units.la: NOBILISSIMO ATQVE ORNATISSIMO VIRO DOMINO PHILIPPO CANAYO Domino à Fraxinis, Regiæ Gall. Maiestatis Consiliario, & eiusdem apud Illustrissimos Germaniæ Principes Legato.
units.tr: TO THE MOST NOBLE AND MOST DISTINGUISHED GENTLEMAN, LORD PHILIPPE CANAYE, Lord of Fraxinis, Councillor to His Majesty the King of France, and his Ambassador to the most illustrious princes of Germany.

units.la: SANÆE, vultu cui placido fauens Phœbus beatos Aonidum dedit Lustrare colles: & profundos Impauidum penetrare clari Saltus Lycei: fas varios tibi Donare versus? fas, age, mittere Quæ nostra conata est Thalia Multiplici resonare plectro? Nam mox cruentos plebis Ibericæ Fastus, & artes dicimus impias: Seu classe bellaces Britannos Terrifica superare tentat. Seu bella Galli ciuica promouet Furentis, illum nec patitur suas Seruare paces, quæritatque
units.tr: Surely, with a face on which Phoebus, favouring it, has granted to wander over the blessed hills of the Aonides, and to enter fearlessly the deep glades of bright Lyceum: is it right to offer you varied verses? Is it right, come, to send what my Thalia has attempted, to resound on a manifold plectrum? For soon we sing of the bloody pride and impious arts of the Iberian people; or when the warlike Britons, with a terrifying fleet, attempt to overcome; or when he fosters the civil wars of raging France, and does not allow it to keep its own peace, and seeks to join the Frankish kingdoms to his own.

units.la: (continued in the next page) Franca suis sociare regna. Mox fata fremus tristia : mox iocos Nugásve amicis innocuas damus : Mox inuidemus fortiorum Facta virum phlegetontis antro. Aut certa vatum praemia pangimus Lauros decoras, aut face mutua Fidum mariti pectus, atque Dona thori pretiosa casti. Nam me per altos quum cytharae potens Duxit tremententem Cynthius Aonas : Fontesque facundos, & antra Castalidum, gracilesque luci Monstrauit vmbras Pierij, & rudem Pulsare molli pollice barbiton, Me plura tunc iussit, modisque Disparibus celebrare carmen: Quod grata Musis pectora dulcibus Auresque possit lenius influens Mulcere doctas, fortiusque Multisono retinere cantu. Sic ficta mixtis ora coloribus Solerte quondam Parrhasius manu Monstrans reportauit superbum
units.tr: Soon we lament the sad fates; soon we give harmless jests and trifles to our friends; soon we envy the deeds of braver men in the cave of Phlegethon. Or we compose the sure rewards of poets, the becoming laurels, or with a mutual torch the faithful heart of a husband and the precious gifts of chaste marriage. For when the Cynthian god, mighty with the lyre, led me trembling over the high Aonian heights, showed me the eloquent fountains and the caves of the Castalides, and the slender shades of the Pierian grove, and bade me, a novice, to strike the lyre with a gentle thumb, then he commanded me to sing many things and to celebrate in various measures a song that might be pleasing to the Muses' tender hearts and might soothe learned ears with a gently flowing sweetness, and hold them more strongly with a many-sounding strain. Thus Parrhasius of old, with skilful hand, displayed a face feigned with mixed colours and carried off the proud glory of a distinguished art as a painter.

units.la: Egregia decus arte pictor. Sic chara mittit pomifero impiger Quæ carpsit anno munera villicus, Quum miscet vuis mella, ficos, Mala, nucem, viridesque olivas. Et lætiores, si rigidæ nouum Ver pigra brumæ frigora dispulit, Per prata diuerso puellæ Serta legunt variata flore. Asttu benigno dispice lumine Quæ pauca dono, seu prius, hospitem Quum nostra te vidit Geneua Læta suum tumidique dulces Ripæ Lemanni: tempore quo ferox Gallis tumultus gens Lothoringica Nouabat: Henricumque dira Fraude suum iugulare regem Tendebat audax: ciuibus vt suis Nudata tellus Francica barbaros Fasces paueret, Baticique Imperio premeretur hostis. Tunc, si sonoræ me studium lyræ Monente dextro cæpit Apolline, Audire cantantem solebas,
units.tr: Thus the diligent farmer sends the dear gifts that he has gathered in the fruit-bearing year, when he mixes grapes with honey, figs, apples, nuts and green olives. And they are more joyful if the sluggish cold of stiff winter has driven away the new spring, when girls gather garlands of varied flowers through the meadows. Look with a kindly eye on the few things I offer you, you who once, as a guest, when our Geneva saw you, were glad, and the sweet banks of the swelling Lake Leman; at the time when the fierce Lorrainers were stirring up tumult against the French, and the bold race was plotting to slay King Henry by dire treachery, so that the French land, stripped of its citizens, might feed barbarian rods, and the enemy be pressed down under Batavian rule. Then, if the study of the resounding lyre began under the guidance of the right-handed Apollo, you used to listen to me as I sang, and to cheer the timid poet with gentle speech.

units.la: Et timidum recreare blandoSermone vatem : Tutior hinc tuoFauore Flacci dulciloquas sequorArtes Venusini, & canorosÆoliæ modulos Camænæ.Hinc dente siquis me petat inuidoTe fretus illum vindice negligam,Linguas procaces, impotensqueArbitrium popularis auræ.
units.tr: Hence, trusting your favour, I shall follow more safely the sweet-speaking arts of Flaccus of Venusia and the tuneful measures of the Aeolian Muse. Hence, if anyone should attack me with a envious tooth, I shall disregard him, relying on you as my avenger: his saucy tongues and his unrestrained judgement, the verdict of the popular breeze.
Devoted to your kindness,
J. Iacomotus B.

units.tr: Verses by Joannes Jacomotus, addressed to Philip Canaeus, a most illustrious man, wreathed with garlands. [ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΙΩΑΝΝΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΙΑΚΩΜΟΤΟΥ Μέλη Φιλίππῳ τῷ Καναίῳ ἀνδρὶ λαμπροτατῳ ἐπιτεφημισμένα.]

units.la: Ἦλθεν Ἰωαννης, (ἀγεῖτο δὲ φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων) Λειμῶν' ἐς Μοισαν, παμπαν ἀεὶ πρεσέα· Λειμῶν' ἀνθεμόεντα, τὸν ὰ Ἠέμις ὄξι βεβήλοις Ὀφθαλμοῖς ἰδέειν, ὐδὲ ποσὶν πατέειν·
units.tr: John came into the meadow of the Muses, which is always very fair (Phoebus Apollo leading him), a flowering meadow that Themis would not let profane eyes behold or profane feet tread. [Ἦλθεν Ἰωαννης, (ἀγεῖτο δὲ φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων) Λειμῶν' ἐς Μοισαν, παμπαν ἀεὶ πρεσέα· Λειμῶν' ἀνθεμόεντα, τὸν ὰ Ἠέμις ὄξι βεβήλοις Ὀφθαλμοῖς ἰδέειν, ὐδὲ ποσὶν πατέειν·]

units.la: Τῷ δ' ἀπὸ δρεψάμενος κἀλὰ πάντοθεν, οἷα μέ- λισσα, Ἀνθεα δώδη, δὲ μάλ' ὅπσα μύρως.
units.tr: Gathering flowers from every side, like a bee, he plucked many blossoms, very many, fragrant with myrrh. [Τῷ δ' ἀπὸ δρεψάμενος κἀλὰ πάντοθεν, οἷα μέλισσα, Ἀνθεα δώδη, δὲ μάλ' ὅπσα μύρως.]

units.la: Σιω ῥόδα, τώτε ἴον, σιω δὲ χραπαν νάκινθον Μίξας, τόνδ' ἐπλεκεν πορφύρεον στέφανον.
units.tr: Mixing roses, violets and hyacinth, he wove them into this purple garland. [Σιω ῥόδα, τώτε ἴον, σιω δὲ χραπαν νάκινθον Μίξας, τόνδ' ἐπλεκεν πορφύρεον στέφανον.]

units.la: Αἴ ψα δ' ἔφη πλέξας, Τίνα δὴ πίναι ἴω δὲ ἠεραί ρω Ηρω, ἡ αν ἐερα χρυσοδέτω στέφει;
units.tr: When he had woven it, he said: "Whom shall I crown with this? Which lovely lady, with golden-bound hair?" [Αἴ ψα δ' ἔφη πλέξας, Τίνα δὴ πίναι ἴω δὲ ἠεραί ρω Ηρω, ἡ αν ἐερα χρυσοδέτω στέφει;]

units.la: Φῆ ὅγε δισάζων· τῷ δ' αἱ Διος αὐτίκα Μῶσαι Φωναν ἐρανόθεν ὠρέχεαν ἀμβροσίαν·
units.tr: So he spoke, in doubt; and at once the Muses, daughters of Zeus, sent down to him an ambrosial voice from heaven. [Φῆ ὅγε δισάζων· τῷ δ' αἱ Διος αὐτίκα Μῶσαι Φωναν ἐρανόθεν ὠρέχεαν ἀμβροσίαν·]

units.la: Ἀμφασιης ὠ λῆγε φίλος· σοὶ δ' εἰξομὲν ἀιμες Δώρον ἀ μέτερον ἀξιος ὃς τελέθει.
units.tr: "Cease your perplexity, dear friend; to you we shall yield the gift, which is worthy of you." [Ἀμφασιης ὠ λῆγε φίλος· σοὶ δ' εἰξομὲν ἀιμες Δώρον ἀ μέτερον ἀξιος ὃς τελέθει.]

units.la: Ἡ ἐχ ὀφάας σὺ, βεργ̃ρ πέλιταις ἑσγτὸς ὃς τις ἄωτος;
units.tr: "Is it not you who, among all the citizens, is the flower and the best of them?" [Ἡ ἐχ ὀφάας σὺ, βεργ̃ρ πέλιταις ἑσγτὸς ὃς τις ἄωτος;]

units.la: Ὃς πινυτῷ πινυτοῖς νῶτον ἐδείξε νόῳ;
units.tr: "You who have shown the way to the wise with a wise mind?" [Ὃς πινυτῷ πινυτοῖς νῶτον ἐδείξε νόῳ;]

units.la: Ὅς Μοίσας φιλέῃ, πεφιλημένος ἔξοχα Μοίσας, (Ἡμετέρων ὀαέων μάρτυς Αρισοτέλης·) Ὅσ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀληθείᾳ πεπλασμένον ἐν Θεῷ ἔρνος, Καὶ κακίαν συγέει, ἠδ᾽ ἀρετῆς ἔεατα· Τῆνον δὴ τῆνον λέγομεν, ᾧ εἰ ἄλλα ΦΙΛΙΠ- ΠΟΝ
units.tr: "You who love the Muses, and are exceedingly beloved of the Muses (our own Aristotle is witness to this), who, a shoot planted in God by truth, cast off vice and embrace virtue: this man, this one, we call Philip..." [Ὅς Μοίσας φιλέῃ, πεφιλημένος ἔξοχα Μοίσας, (Ἡμετέρων ὀαέων μάρτυς Αρισοτέλης·) Ὅσ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀληθείᾳ πεπλασμένον ἐν Θεῷ ἔρνος, Καὶ κακίαν συγέει, ἠδ᾽ ἀρετῆς ἔεατα· Τῆνον δὴ τῆνον λέγομεν, ᾧ εἰ ἄλλα ΦΙΛΙΠ- ΠΟΝ]

units.la: Καὶ φίλον ἀνθρώποις, ἠὲ φίλον ἀθανάτοις. Τόσσα θεαί μοι ἔβαξαν· ὁ δ᾽ ἐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀ- κέσας.
units.tr: "and dear to men, or dear to the immortals." So much the goddesses told me, and he, having heard, did not disbelieve. [Καὶ φίλον ἀνθρώποις, ἠὲ φίλον ἀθανάτοις. Τόσσα θεαί μοι ἔβαξαν· ὁ δ᾽ ἐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκέσας.]

units.la: Ἀλλὰ Καναῖε τεῖν τόνδε φέρει στέφανον. Δέξαι, δ᾽ ὦ μέγ᾽ ἀείσε, θέλων· ἠχαίρεε ἄμφω, Ἄμφω ὑμετέρᾳ μνάμονες Ισαάκ.
units.tr: "But, Canaeus, this garland is brought to you. Accept it, great singer, willingly; rejoice, both of you, both mindful of your Isaac." [Ἀλλὰ Καναῖε τεῖν τόνδε φέρει στέφανον. Δέξαι, δ᾽ ὦ μέγ᾽ ἀείσε, θέλων· ἠχαίρεε ἄμφω, Ἄμφω ὑμετέρᾳ μνάμονες Ισαάκ.]
Isaacus Casaubonus.

units.la: AD IOAN. IACOMOTVM Barrensem amicissimum, & in Ecclesia Geneuensi verbi Dei ministrum Th. Quatigranus Tempensis hoc μνη-μόσυνον dabat.
units.tr: To Joannes Jacomotus of Bar, his dearest friend and minister of the Word of God in the Church of Geneva: Th. Quatigranus of Tempe gave this memorial [μνημόσυνον].

units.la: DElius Aonio decorat pede dū sacros poetas, Orbemque ducit versibus decentem: Et nitida meritum gestit caput impedire lauro, Superbientis præmio coronæ: Plurima demissum resonat lyra, nec graues la-borum, Pacisque belliquæ vrget officinas: Ereptósve duces Orco inuidet, auream perita Ciere chordam vocibus canoris.
units.tr: Since you adorn the sacred poets with the Aonian foot, and lead the world with verses fit for it, your shining head eagerly seeks to be crowned with laurel, the reward of a proud wreath. Your lyre sounds many themes, not only the heavy labours but also the workshops of peace and war. You envy the leaders snatched from Orcus, for you are skilled at stirring the golden string with tuneful voices.

units.la: At properat tibi, Phœbus amicior, implicare frontem Æterne vates laurea comante. Cuius deleuit reliquas nitor inuidendus, alma Vt nocte lucei sÿderum minores Inter pura faces Latonia. Principum, nec alter Maiore plectro cædibus madentes Pugnas edit,& arua liquentia, perfido cruore Infecta: nec non arte parricidas Multiplici, merito diru in caput ante coparatam Tulisse Gallo vindici procellam. Maturat poenas domino scelus,& propinqua turpes Vrgent ministros criminum flagella. Nec maius Clariis vnquam decus ambulauit oris Quàm si bonorum laude sempiterna Culpae supplicium veniat comes,auribusque natae Musae loquantur quae premant scelestos.
units.tr: But Phoebus, more kindly disposed, hastens to bind your brow, eternal poet, with the laurel that adorns it. Its enviable brilliance outshines all the rest, as the Latonian light, the kindly night's brightest, outshines the lesser stars among the pure torches of heaven. No other poet, with a greater plectrum, sings of princes, of battles drenched in slaughter, of fields running with treacherous blood and polluted with it. Nor does any other, with manifold art, describe the parricides, or the storm that deservedly fell on the head of the Gaul, long prepared as an avenger. Crime hastens its punishment upon its lord, and the scourges of nearby shame press hard on the ministers of wickedness. Greater glory has never walked on the lips of the Clarii than when the punishment of guilt comes as the companion of the everlasting praise of good men, and the Muses speak in the ears of the daughters so as to crush the wicked.

units.la: TRIVMPHALE CARMEN, AD SERENISSIMAM Angliæ Reginam.
units.tr: TRIUMPHAL SONG, TO THE MOST SERENE QUEEN OF ENGLAND.

units.la: OVÆ penna, quauis ocyor alite, Raptum per altos me feret ætheris Tractus, Britannorumq; sistet Finibus incolumem remotis?
units.tr: O, on a wing swifter than any bird, will it carry me, snatched through the high tracts of the air, and set me down unharmed on the far-off borders of Britain?

units.la: Vt læta fractis littora puppibus, Vrbésque festas hostibus obrutis Regina, cernam, qui catenas, Qui tibi perniciem parabant!
units.tr: That I may see, O Queen, the joyful shores, the ships broken, and the festive cities, the enemies overwhelmed, who were preparing chains and ruin for you!

units.la: Heu, heu, Britannis quanta ferox tuis Miles movebat funera Ibericus, Quum classe per vastum superbus Terrifica volitab at æquor!
units.tr: Alas, alas, what great funerals the fierce Spanish soldier was stirring up for your Britons, when, proud in his fleet, he flew terrifying across the vast sea!

units.la: Non ante Graias pluribus insolens Constrauit oras Persa triremibus, Quum frena Neptuno minatus Argolicis dare iura vellet.
units.tr: The Persian, unaccustomed to such things, had never before crowded the Greek shores with so many triremes, when, threatening to give bridles to Neptune, he wished to impose laws on the Argives.

units.la: Non ante plures Actia littoraVidere nautas, quum Pharias potensAugustus Ægypti cohortesViribus imperij reuicit.
units.tr: Never before did the Actian shores see so many sailors, when Augustus, powerful, overcame by the strength of his empire the Pharian cohorts of Egypt.

units.la: Te diua, ditem quaregis AngliamSeruat benigni gratia Numinis,Tutela, & aduersis fidelePræsidium columénque rebus.
units.tr: You, goddess, who keep rich England under the grace of a kindly divinity, are its protection, its defence and its pillar in adverse affairs, faithful to it.

units.la: Quòd mœsta, squallens, supplice dextera,Vultúsque largis fletibus obruensCum plebe ieiuna minantemDamna Deum precibus serenas.
units.tr: Because you, sad and squalid, with suppliant right hand and face overwhelmed with copious tears, together with the hungry people, calm with prayers the God who threatens damnation.

units.la: Quid vera possit Religio piisArmata votis, quid valeant preces,Testatur Hispani cruorePurpureum pereuntis æquor.
units.tr: What true religion can do, armed with prayers for the pious, and what prayers avail, the sea, purpled with the blood of the perishing Spaniard, bears witness.

units.la: Disiecta Ponto corpora, nauiumMoles stupenda, gazaque nobilisCaptiua testatur, DucúmqueNunc domitus furor impotentum.
units.tr: The bodies scattered on the sea, the stupendous mass of ships, and the noble captured treasure bear witness, and now the impotent fury of the raging ones is tamed.

units.la: His Angla pubes auspiciis valensNon sustinendo sæuiit impetu,Classisque deiecit minaces,Marte pio furiata, fastus,
units.tr: By these auspices the English youth, strong, raged with an onset that could not be withstood, and the fleet cast down the threatening pride, maddened by pious war.

units.la: Vrsitque remis, accipiter velutMolles columbas, quos fuga certiorÆquor per incertum triumphisSurripuit properata iustis.
units.tr: And it pressed on with oars, as a hawk presses soft doves; the sea, uncertain, snatched them away in triumph, hurried by just means, more certain than flight.

units.la: Addicta quondam progenies DeoSic fudit hostis acrior impios, Victrixque, dum Moses fidelis Tendit ad astra manus precantes.
units.tr: Once the people devoted to God were thus poured out by a fiercer enemy as impious; and they were victorious, while faithful Moses stretched his hands in prayer toward the heavens.

units.la: Consulta veri quod SapientiaSemper minorem Numine te geris, Regni, vinces, hostibusque Sceptra feres metuenda cunctis.
units.tr: Since you, consulting the truth, always bear yourself as lesser than the divine power, O Queen, you will conquer your kingdom, and you will bear a sceptre to be feared by all enemies.

units.la: AEternus orbis nam tibi militatRector, furentes qui quatit improbos, Virésque vasanas retundit Omne nefas animo moventes.
units.tr: For the eternal ruler of the world fights on your side, he who shakes the raging wicked and crushes the mighty forces of every crime that stir in their minds.

units.la: Quite benigno lumine respicit,Tutámque praestat: qui vigil excubat, Et fraudis authores recludens Insidias referat latentes.
units.tr: He looks upon you with a kindly light and grants you safety; he who keeps watch vigilant, and unveiling the authors of fraud, will reveal the hidden plots.

units.la: Insanientum te quibus impetit,Turbátque liuor Pontificum irritus, Omnisque coniurata veros Perdere Christicolas caterua.
units.tr: Against those madmen who attack you, and against the envy of the Pontiffs, vain though it be, which disturbs you, and every conspiring band that seeks to destroy the true Christians.

units.la: Te victus auro nunc parat artifexMiscere mensis toxica regiis Maltare, ni tutela Christi Fraude pium caput expediret.
units.tr: Now a craftsman, bought with gold, prepares to mix poisons into the royal dishes and to slay you, unless Christ's protection, by its cunning, had freed your pious head.

units.la: Nunc Iesuites seditionibusPaces Britanni vertere ciuicis Molitur almas, téque tentat Legitimis spoliare sceptris.
units.tr: Now the Jesuits, by sedition, plot to overturn the sweet peace of the British citizens, and they try to strip you of your legitimate sceptres.

units.la: Captúsque grandi munere mittiturAugusta sacra limina qui domusPerrupit audax, & retectoEnse tuum latus appetiuit.Hac arte Princeps concidit Auricus,Quo dura fortes vindice vinculaRupere Belga, quum TyrannusIussit Iber violare leges,Iurata Genti fœdera subruens.Hæc Roma monstrat perfida, quæ fidemPactámque dextram ChristianisFraude noua temerare sancit.Cur pace s:cla, Tygride seuior,Heu Roma quæris sub iuga mittereHispana bellaces Britannos,Innocuúmque caput fatigas?Vrit profanos fœmina PræsulesDilecta calo, cui placet obsequiChristo docenti: cuíque cordi estArdua cum pietate Virtus.Vrit cruentis quod cruciatibusDulcem coactos linquere PatriamSolatur, & Christum sequutosHospitiis recreat benignis.Quòd fida sacros auxiliis gregesFirmat piorum non trepidantibus.Longósque Belgarum laboresMarte potens miserata sanat.
units.tr: The man who, captured by a great reward, is sent, and who audaciously broke through the sacred thresholds of the Augusta's house and, with bared sword, sought your side. By this art the Prince Auricus fell, by which the Belgians, under a fierce avenger, broke hard chains, when the Spanish tyrant ordered the laws to be violated, undermining the covenant sworn to the nation. This is what faithless Rome shows, which sanctions the violation of faith and of the pledged right hand of Christians by new fraud. Why, Rome, more cruel than a tigress, do you seek to send the warlike Britons under the Spanish yoke, and harass the innocent head? The woman beloved of heaven burns the profane prelates, she who delights to obey Christ teaching, and to whose heart lofty virtue is dear along with piety. She consoles those forced to leave their homeland by cruel tortures, and refreshes with kindly hospitality those who follow Christ. She faithfully strengthens with aid the sacred flocks of the pious, who do not tremble, and with pity, powerful in war, she heals the long labours of the Belgians.

units.la: Quòd Veritatis feruida candidæIgnes per orbem spargere lucidos:Et fraudis inuisas fugareTartareas meditatur umbras.
units.tr: Which, zealous, longs to spread the bright fires of the candid Truth throughout the world, and to put to flight the hated shadows of fraud and of Tartarus.

units.la: O TAM celebri nunc ter & ampliusRegnata felix Anglia Principe!O nunc triumphatis IberumNobilior ducibus superbis!
units.tr: O happy England, now reigning thrice and more with so celebrated a Prince! O now nobler than the proud leaders of the Spaniards, who have been vanquished!

units.la: Nunc nunc Britanni Cœlituum PatremLaudare tempus, nunc fora, compita,Et templa, diuinos fauoresPerpetuo resonate canu.
units.tr: Now, now, Britons, is the time to praise the Father of the heavenly beings; now let the forums, the crossroads and the temples resound with divine favours in perpetual song.

units.la: Lucémque sistam, quæ redeuntibusRidebit annis semper Adoreâ:Quæ fudit Hispanos potentesPer memores celebrate fastos.
units.tr: And I shall establish a festival that will smile every returning year as Adorea; celebrate it through memorable annals, the festival that poured out the mighty Spaniards.

units.la: Fas & fauenti plaudere murmureQuos cura Christi prouida sustinetCùm frangit hostes, cùm nefandæTurba perit truculenta gentis.
units.tr: It is right to applaud, with favouring murmur, those whom Christ's provident care sustains, when he breaks the enemies, when the savage crowd of the unholy race perishes.

units.la: Quacunque lucis conscia OlympicæTerras per omnes æthereum colis,Gens sacra patrem fœderatisPectoribus sociate vota.
units.tr: Wherever you dwell throughout all lands, conscious of the Olympic light, O holy nation, unite your prayers to the Father with allied hearts.

units.la: Ut tanta cunctis sospes ab hostibusRegina, vitæ tempora prorogansFelicis, Antiquos BritannosImperiis moderetur æquis.
units.tr: That the Queen, safe from all enemies, may prolong the times of her happy life and rule the ancient Britons with an equitable empire.
So that she may shine with praise for later generations
and grow in splendour, no less than her forebears,
by the virtue of her ancestors, may the
mighty in arms increase her proud triumphs,
and, ever stronger, restrain the impious wrath
of the giants, while the faithless and gloomy ones
rise up when the fury will stir against the truth
the wars of the mitred flock.

units.la: NEREI VATICINIVM DE Ruina classis Ibericae.
units.tr: NEREUS' PROPHECY CONCERNING THE RUIN OF THE SPANISH FLEET.

units.la: OVVM Gentis tumidus rector Iberica Audaci peteret classe Britannicum Littus: quum celebres turpia tenderet Anglos sub iuga mittere:
units.tr: When the proud ruler of the Iberian nation was making for the British shore with a bold fleet, meaning to bring the famous English under a shameful yoke:

units.la: Ingratum cupidis navibus ocium Turbato posuit Nereus aequore, Praevisas cecinit dum properantibus Clades, fataque proxima.
units.tr: Nereus stirred the sea and ended the unwelcome idleness of the eager ships. While they hurried on, he sang of the disasters foreseen and the fates close at hand.

units.la: Lugubri patrias deseris alite Oras, Classis, ait. Quo ruis impetu Praeceps? O, quid agis? fortiter occupa Portum. Nunc quid Ibericis
units.tr: "You leave your native shores on a mournful wing, O fleet," he said. "Where are you rushing headlong with such force? Oh, what are you doing? Bravely seize the harbour.

units.la: Regnis regna paras Anglica iungere?Intentata tuis littora puppibus,Bellacésque animos Marte lacessere,Cæcus quem furor incitat?
units.tr: Why do you prepare to join the kingdom of England to the kingdoms of Iberia? Why do you, blinded by the madness that drives you, plan to assail shores your ships have never touched and to provoke a people fierce in war?

units.la: Non tu bella geres mollia cum gregeImbelli facilis victor Americo:Quæ gens rudá tuos non tulit impetus,Armorum, & rudis agminum.
units.tr: You will not wage a soft war against an unwarlike crowd, an easy victor over the Americans. What people, raw and untrained in arms and ranks, has not endured your assaults?

units.la: Sic ieiuna lupum quum stimulat fames,Sævit lanigeros impiger in greges,Sic pullos rapidis Miluus unguibusImpiumes lacerat ferox.
units.tr: As when hunger, starving, goads the wolf, and it rages eagerly among the woolly flocks, or as the kite, fierce, tears apart the unfledged chicks with swift talons.

units.la: Heu non fausta moues bella BritannicæGenti: cum rigidis prælia conseresAngli pectoribus cedere nescij:Iustus quem furor asperat,
units.tr: Alas, you bring no fortunate wars upon the British nation, whose men do not know how to yield, and who join battle with stiff breasts. The just fury of the English is roused

units.la: Hostes quum patriis finibus excutit,Quum pro sollicitis dimicat acriorMiles coniugibus, vincula quum timetNatis barbara dulcibus.
units.tr: when it drives the enemy out of their native borders, when the soldier fights more fiercely for his anxious wives, when he fears chains for his dear children at barbarian hands.

units.la: Non Hircana furit Tigris acerbius,Getulúsve Leo saepius infremit,Quum seruat catulos, denteque quum vagumRaptorem laniat truci.
units.tr: The Hyrcanian tigress does not rage more bitterly, nor does the Getulian lion roar more often, when it guards its cubs and tears the roving plunderer with savage tooth.

units.la: Quantum Marte queat nobilis AngliaInuicto & proauis inclita LaureisTestes damna tuis plurima quæ deditOlim, Gallia, regibus.
units.tr: How much England, noble in war and famed for her ancestral laurels, can do, you, France, can bear witness, for she once inflicted many losses on your kings.

units.la: Testes sæpe tuis æquoribus rates Fractæ, puniceo sanguine decolor Pontus, luctificis oppida subruta Flammis, captáque mœnia. Nónne obsessa vides littora milite Anglo cuncta, simul navibus obrutos Fluctus innumeris, vela minantia, Telorum strepitus graues, Ignémque Aeolio sulphure feruidum, Clades ferre tuis puppibus asperas Doctum? Nonne vides impavidas Ducum Mentes, exitium tuæ Gentis? Cerne piam pectore prouido Reginam, procerum consiliis sacris Erectam, ut trepidæ strenua patriæ Duris rebus opem ferat. Sic qui puppe sedens celsior imperat Nautarum pavidas sedulus excitat Mentes, si scopulos cautus, & Africi Vitat præcipites minas: Castigátque moras, quum maris impiger Iratí tumidos murmura tollere Fluctus, séque diem condere percipit Nimbis tristibus obrutum. Sic pastor vigiles sollicitat canum Prudens excubias, quum gregibus timet Infirmis, avidos quum trepidantibus Propellit stabulis lupos.
units.tr: Witness the ships often broken on your seas, the sea discoloured with purple blood, towns overthrown by mournful flames, and captured walls. Do you not see the shores on every side beset by English soldiers, the waves overwhelmed with ships, the sails threatening, the harsh clamour of weapons, and fire glowing with Aeolian sulphur, which, as the learned say, brings harsh disasters upon your ships? Do you not see the undaunted minds of the commanders, the ruin of your nation? Behold the pious queen with her far-sighted heart, raised up by the sacred counsels of her nobles, so that she may bring vigorous help to her fearful country in hard times. So he who sits higher on the stern gives orders and diligently rouses the fearful minds of the sailors, if he cautiously avoids the rocks and the headlong threats of the southwest wind; and he rebukes delays when he perceives the sea tossing its swelling waves, and the day overwhelmed by gloomy storm clouds, ready to hide itself. So the wise shepherd diligently rouses the vigilant watch of his dogs when he fears for his weak flocks, when he drives the greedy wolves from the trembling stalls.

units.la: Heu, heu, quantus adest militibus tuisSudor! Quanta mones funera IbericaGenti. Quanta ferox Angla triremibusPubes damna tuis feret!
units.tr: Alas, alas, how great a sweat awaits your soldiers! What deaths you threaten for the Iberian people! How great the losses the fierce English youth will inflict on your triremes!

units.la: Te mox fulmineo turbine glandiumQuassabit, rutilis te petet ignibus,Incendétque simul lintea, remiges,Malos, transtráque nauium,Spumantésque tuo sanguine gurgitesInfecisse ferigestiet æquoris.Ridebit spoliis auctus Americis,Auro ditior Indico.
units.tr: Soon he will shake you with a thunderbolt-like whirl of bullets, seek you out with ruddy fires, and at the same time set alight your sails, oarsmen, masts and the thwarts of your ships, and he will eagerly stain the foaming waves of the sea with your blood. He will laugh, enriched with American spoils and richer in gold than the Indies.

units.la: Nequicquam æquoreos perdita tunc rogaDiuos, supplicibus pietáve numinaVotis sollicita. Non miseræ precesDuris mortibus eximent.
units.tr: In vain then, lost, you will beg the sea gods, and the divinities, with anxious prayers and the piety of suppliants. Your wretched prayers will not free you from cruel deaths.

units.la: Nequicquam fugient hostibus impares,Et duris lacera vulneribus rates.Nequicquam latebras Oceano petent.Exsfes nil fuga proderit.
units.tr: In vain will your ships, unequal to the enemy and mangled by harsh wounds, try to flee. In vain will they seek hiding places in the ocean. Flight will avail you nothing.

units.la: Si vicina petis littora Belgy,Parmensemque vocas praesidio Ducem,Te pellet Batauus miles acerbior,Hispani metuens iugi.
units.tr: If you seek the neighbouring shores of Belgium and call the Duke of Parma to your aid, the Batavian soldier, fiercer still, will drive you away, fearing the Spanish yoke.

units.la: Est Anglis stabili fœdere DaniaIuncta, & quæ latitant tecta TrionibusSeptenis profugos æquora negligunt,Tutúmque hospitium negant
units.tr: Denmark is joined to the English by a firm covenant, and the seas that hide the houses of the Seven Triones neglect fugitives and deny a safe hospitality.
If you ask about the kingdoms subject to the fierce Scots,
If you ask about the Orkneys, famous for shipwrecks, with your ships mutilated,
Thirty of them, you will come to,
If you plough the Irish sea,
All these shores are hostile to your ships:
Here you see the sea with rapid whirlpools, and
Treacherous with rocks, and roaring
With perpetual north winds.
At last, long a plaything for the fickle winds
And aimless toils,
A pitiable fall, overthrown
Far off, on the Spanish sea.

units.la: INDISTICHON AB EITZINGERO QVODAM aduersus Reginam Angliæ scriptum.
units.tr: COUPLET WRITTEN BY A CERTAIN EITZINGER AGAINST THE QUEEN OF ENGLAND.
Such is the couplet.

units.la: TV, quæ Romanas voluisti spernere leges, Hispano discés subdere colla iugo.
units.tr: You, who wished to scorn the Roman laws, will learn to submit your neck to the Spanish yoke.
REPLY.

units.la: DVra ferox Anglis quum vincla pararet Iberus, Indomitósque truci classe domare viros: Misit Tartarei scitatum oracula Ditis. (Sic Magica bellum tutior arte gerit.) Huic Dæmon, Aio te vincere posse Britannos, Et premere immani colla superba iugo. Arripit has sortes, & sic exponit Iberus, Hispano subdes colla Britanne iugo. At Iber ambigua deceptus sorte, secures Anglorum metuit vincula dura ferens. Sic regnum Croesi & magnam peruertit opum vim Dæmon, & Pyrrhum perdidit Æacidem.
units.tr: When fierce Iberia was preparing chains for the English and planned to subdue their unconquered men with a savage fleet, it sent to seek the oracles of Tartarean Dis. (Thus magic wages war more safely.) The demon answered: "I say that you can conquer the Britons and press their proud necks under a monstrous yoke." Iberia seized these lots and interpreted them thus: "Britain, you will submit your neck to the Spanish yoke." But Iberia, deceived by the ambiguous lot, dreads the axes and harsh chains of the English. So the demon overthrew the kingdom of Croesus and the great might of his wealth, and destroyed Pyrrhus the son of Aeacus.

units.la: IN ITALOS, QVI FALSO RVMORE DECEPTI τῷ τῆς νίκης ἐγκώμιον celebrarunt.
units.tr: AGAINST THE ITALIANS, WHO, DECEIVED BY A FALSE RUMOUR, CELEBRATED WITH A PANEGYRIC THE VICTORY [τῷ τῆς νίκης ἐγκώμιον]

units.la: Vix praeceps Italis recitarat fama Britannos Hesperio victos milite Martigenas: Ecce suis festos accedunt urbibus ignes, Atque strepunt laetis compita cuncta choris. Omnibus ipse sua Romanus praesul ab arce Primus latina maxima signa dedit. Non mirum est Italos si mendax fama sagaces Fallat, Romuleum fallit & illa Iouem.
units.tr: Scarcely had rumour reported the Britons, the sons of Mars, conquered by the Spanish soldier, when behold, bonfires blazed in their towns in celebration, and every crossroads rang with joyful dances. Before them all, the Roman prelate himself, from his citadel, first gave the great Latin signal. It is no wonder that the Italians, however shrewd, are deceived by a lying rumour, since that same rumour deceived Jupiter of Rome as well.

units.la: HISPANIS VETITVM NE CLADEM AMISSÆ CLASSIS lugerent.
units.tr: The Spaniards are forbidden to mourn the disaster of their lost fleet.

units.la: Cur non dura suæ flet funera classis Iberus? Cur non iusta facit? cur negat exequias? Barbara gens nescit lachrymas, nec iura sepulchri: Námque illi duro mens adamante riget.
units.tr: Why does the Iberian not weep for the deaths of his fleet? Why does he not perform the due rites? Why does he refuse funeral honours? That barbarous nation knows no tears, nor the rights of the tomb, for its mind is hardened as though by hard adamant.

units.la: AD CLARISSIMVM VIRVM IACOBVM LECTIVM Iurisconsultum, cùm ad illum superiores versus legendos misisset.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man James Lectius, jurist, when he had sent him the earlier verses to read.

units.la: CVr tibi quem primos inter numeramus amicos Carmina postremo nostra legenda damus? Consultum Iuris ne lite moremur iniqua, Lecti, peccatum rusticitate vides.
units.tr: Why do we give you our latest poems to read, you whom we count among our first friends? Lest we keep a jurist busy with an unjust lawsuit, Lectius, you see the fault of my rustic clumsiness.
The reply of Lectius.

units.la: SErus vbi solidam reddit cum fœnore sortem Debitor, ista mihi non male grata mora est: Atqui non sortem, non vllum fœnus amico Debueras vltro pendis vtrunque tamen. Illa voco sortem maiore sonanda cothurno. Fœnus versiculi sunt mihi nempe tui.
units.tr: When a debtor late in paying returns the solid principal with interest, that delay is not unwelcome to me. Yet you did not owe me the principal, nor any interest as a friend, and still you pay both. I call those the principal, to be sounded in a loftier buskin. The interest, of course, are your little verses for me.

units.la: IN GALLOS BELLIS CIVI- libus æstuantes.
units.tr: To the Gauls, seething with civil wars.

units.la: QVid motus renouas, Gallia, ciuicos? Quid gentis propriæ funera cernere Gestis, delicias pacis, & ocij Longas indocilis pati?
units.tr: Why do you renew civil strife, Gaul? Why do you delight to behold the deaths of your own people, and, untaught, to endure long years without peace or leisure?

units.la: Si te bella iuuant, in tua sit nefas Enses te proprios condere viscera, Ciuilíque domos oppida, flumina, & Agros tingere sanguine.
units.tr: If wars delight you, let it be your crime to plunge your own swords into your own entrails, and to stain your cities, towns, rivers and fields with citizens' blood.

units.la: Quæsitum pro auis ergo laboribus Regnum, postgeniti seditionibus Vertent indigenis? maximáque imperi Tandem gloria corruet?
units.tr: Will the kingdom won by your ancestors' labours be handed over to natives by the sedition of your descendants? Will the greatest glory of your empire at last collapse?

units.la: Quam non Teutonico soedere firmior Hispanus potuit perdere, nec ferox Anglus, Marte licet sæpe potentior, Nec tristes Italûm doli, Coniurata suis Gallia viribus A se victa ruet? Sævius extero Cives hoste suos immiserabiles Perdet Gallicus heu furor?
units.tr: Will Gaul, conspiring against her own strength and overthrown by herself, fall, when the Spaniard, firmer than any German treaty, could not destroy her, nor the fierce Englishman, though often mightier in war, nor the sad tricks of the Italians? Will Gallic fury, more savage than a foreign enemy, destroy its own citizens without pity?

units.la: Fœdatos patrio sanguine turpiter Natorum gladios, matréque Colchica
units.tr: The swords of sons shamefully befouled with fatherland blood, and the Colchian mother

units.la: Peiores licuit cernere FrancicasMatres, credite posteri.
units.tr: Let posterity believe: you could see French mothers worse than she.

units.la: Fraternis maduit caedibus horridaTellus, nulla fides nec pietas thoriSeruauere viros, matris ab vbereDistractus periit puer.
units.tr: The horrid land has been soaked with fraternal slaughter; no faith or piety has kept men to their marriage vows; a boy was torn from his mother's breast and perished.

units.la: Non seuit catulis Tigris acerbiusRaptis, ira neque est tanta Leonibus,Quum praedam lacerant unguibus, aut lupusPugnas si monet Impares.
units.tr: The tigress does not rage more fiercely against her cubs when they are snatched away, nor is the wrath of lions so great when they tear their prey with claws, nor the wolf's when it provokes unequal fights.

units.la: Expertus toties Gallica quid feroVirtus marte queat, nunc posuit metum,Nunc tantis fruitur cladibus ItalusGallorum exuviis nitens.
units.tr: Tested so often, what can Gallic valour do in war? Now the Italian has put fear aside, and now he enjoys such great slaughter, glittering in the spoils of the Gauls.

units.la: Gallos sique suis vulneribus videtAttritos, merito miles Ibericus,Quos olim timuit nunc sine pulvereSperat cogere sub iugum.
units.tr: If the Spanish soldier sees the Gauls worn down by their own wounds, he rightly hopes to force under the yoke, without any dust of battle, those whom he once feared.

units.la: Securusque tuis Gallia motibus,Oras splendidior nomen in ultimasExtendit Dominus, victor & insolensCunctis regibus imperat:
units.tr: And Gaul, secure in your upheavals, the Lord extends your name to the furthest shores, more splendid, and the victor, insolent, commands all kings:

units.la: Quacunque exoriens sol habitabilesTerras eximio lumine recreat,Et quā regna virūm maximè agrestiumCelabat prius occidens.
units.tr: Wherever the rising sun refreshes the inhabited lands with its splendid light, and wherever the setting sun once hid the kingdoms of the rustic peoples.

units.la: Armis arua tuis debita possidetHispanus, Latiis culta ligonibus,
units.tr: The Spaniard possesses fields owed to your arms, tilled with Latin hoes.

units.la: Hoc victore feret Belga iugum, tuis Olim legibus obsequens.
units.tr: Under this victor the Belgian will bear the yoke, once obedient to your laws.

units.la: Si te Martis amor tam rapit impotens Telis saeuus Iber quae sibi vendicat, Iniustis, Itali quae simul occupant: Fas est, Marte reposcito.
units.tr: If the unbridled love of Mars so seizes you, let the cruel Iberian be made to give back, by war, what he claims with weapons and what the Italians likewise occupy by unjust right: it is right to reclaim it by war.

units.la: Alpes perpetuis quae niuibus rigent, Quae summo feriunt nubila vertice, Non gentis poterunt frangere Gallicae Iunctum robur & impetum.
units.tr: The Alps, stiff with perpetual snows, which strike the clouds with their highest peaks, will not be able to break the united strength and onset of the Gallic race.

units.la: Non rex Eridanus, turbaque fluminum, Non arces validis rupibus insita, Gallos Ausoniae finibus arceant Iustus si furor incitat.
units.tr: Neither the king Eridanus, nor the crowd of rivers, nor citadels set on sturdy rocks will keep the Gauls from the borders of Ausonia, if righteous fury stirs them.

units.la: Si vicina fugis, quae procul afferent Lauros, & meritam bella superbiam Aude, fama iubet, milite Turcicam Gallo frange potentiam.
units.tr: If you shun what is near, which brings laurels and deserved pride in war from afar, dare, fame bids you: with Gallic soldiers, break the power of the Turks.

units.la: Teflens Imperiis subdita Barbaris Expectat rigidum Graecia vindicem.
units.tr: Greece, subjected to barbarian rule, awaits a stern avenger.

units.la: Te vastatus ager fertilis Africa, Te pingues Asia vocant.
units.tr: Fertile Africa, her fields laid waste, and rich Asia call you.

units.la: Est virtus miseros soluere vinculis Quorum colla premit libera seruitus: Haec laus digna tuo nomine te manet, Francis dignaque Regibus.
units.tr: It is a virtue to loose from their chains the wretched whose necks harsh slavery presses down: this praise awaits you, worthy of your name and worthy of the kings of the Franks.

units.la: Hanc quaesisse iuuet sanguine, quem parant Ciuilis furiae fundere diffidl: Hostes perde, licet: sed pietas iubetCives parcere civibus.
units.tr: Let it please you to seek this with blood, which civil fury prepares to pour out. Destroy your enemies, if you will; but piety bids citizens spare citizens.

units.la: AD ORNATISS. VIRVM D. Iac. LECTIVM IVRISCONS. & Senatorem reipub. Genevensis clarissimum.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Master James Lectius, jurisconsult and most famous senator of the Republic of Geneva.

units.la: MVsis amico carmina LectioQuae pauca tandem mittitLongam salutem nuntiateEt bene rem gerere & valere.Ast occupatum si gravioribusCernetis illum forte negotiis:Iustamque causam si clientisPromovet auxilium petentis.Si iura tractat, si Senecam mageSolatur aegrum vulnere sontico,Plagosa scriptorum quod olimTurba manu tulit insolente:Propensiori ne studio precorPeccate nostri, commoda temporaServate, dimisso SenatuSive domum redit ociosus,Coenam libellis sive petit brevemServus relictis, tunc vacat arbitror Audire nugantes amicos,
units.tr: To the friend of the Muses, Lectius, I send these few verses at last, announcing long greetings and that you are doing well and faring well. But if you see him busy with more serious business, or if he gives aid to a just cause of a client who seeks it; if he handles the law, or if he consoles the sick man with Seneca rather than with the wound of the sore which once a crowd of writers brought with insolent hand: I pray, with more eager zeal, that you keep our times favourable, when he returns home at leisure after the Senate is dismissed, or when, a servant having left his books, he asks for a short dinner; then, I think, he has time to listen to his chattering friends.
Then he drives away gloomy cares.
If he receives you with kindly light,
Offer tears, which your
Prince Condé, death by poisons
Hastened by untamed hands, ordered.

units.la: DEPLORATIO INOBITVM TRISTISSIMVM ILLVSTRISsimi Principis Condæi, Henrici Borbonij veneno sublati.
units.tr: Lament for the most sad death of the most illustrious Prince Condé, Henry of Bourbon, carried off by poison.

units.la: ORBONICÆ cecidit gentis fortißimus Heros, Dolis petitus Colchicis: Quem non perpetuis potuerunt perdere bellis, Iræ potentes Principum: Quem non aduersæ trepidum videre phalanges, Periculisque territum: Quem nulla hostilis vicit victoria, fortem Per damna quæuis crescere. Imbelles animas, ignauáque pectora, Francûm Pudenda carcinomata, Vos superis perdat iaculatus ab arcibus ignes Deus rubente dextera.
units.tr: The bravest hero of the Bourbon race has fallen, sought out by Colchian tricks: whom the powerful anger of princes could not destroy in perpetual wars; whom hostile battle lines did not see trembling, nor terrified by danger; whom no enemy victory conquered, a man who grew stronger through any losses. Cowardly souls and idle hearts, shameful cancers of the Franks, may God, hurling fire from the high citadels with a blazing right hand, destroy you.

units.la: Hoc vobis licuisse nefas? extinguere tantum Atro veneno Principem? Thessalicis ergo insidiis, atque artibus, omnis Sanguis peribit Regius? Gallica sic visum est aconitis sceptra parare Seu poculis Canidiae? Tam vos regnandi rapuit vesana libido, & Caeci furoris impetus, Legibus ut spretis, nulla virtute, venenis, Periuriis & cadibus, Legitimis tandem pulsis haeredibus, eheu! Gallos regatis aduenae? Ah, Galli, quae vos cepit dementia! tantus Vos vsque vexabit furor? Illis ut regni tristes prodatis habenas, Artes malae quos prouehunt? Scilicet his meritum grati referetis honorem, Laudisque auitae praemia. Scilicet auxerunt vestros virtute triumphos, Auxere vestra commoda. Ecce, Periclaeo paces stratagemate, turbant, Mutantque bellis ocia. Ciuiles ecce accendunt ad praelia dextras, Martemque inexpiabilem. En cives crebris attritos cladibus ista, Exhauriunt Hirudines. Francisci frustra mens cauit prouida Regis, Haec ominata posteris.
units.tr: Was this crime allowed you, to extinguish a prince with black poison? So by Thessalian plots and arts all royal blood will perish? Did it seem good to the Gauls to prepare the sceptre with aconite, or with the cups of Canidia? Did such mad lust for reigning seize you, and the blind onrush of frenzy, so that, with laws scorned and no virtue, by poisons, perjuries and slaughter, the legitimate heirs being driven out, alas, you would be ruled by foreigners? Ah, Gauls, what madness has seized you! Will so great a fury vex you without end? That you should hand the sad reins of the kingdom to those whom evil arts promote? Surely you will repay them with the reward of grateful honour and the prizes of ancestral praise. Surely they have increased your triumphs by their valour, increased your advantages. Behold, by a dangerous stratagem they disturb the peace and exchange leisure for war. Behold, they kindle civil right hands to battle, and an inexpiable Mars. Lo, the leeches drain citizens already worn down by repeated disasters. In vain the provident mind of King Francis took care, foretelling these things to posterity.

units.la: Nati, Guisiadas, fatalia nomina, dixit,Arcete vestris finibus.
units.tr: "Sons, keep the Guises away from your borders," he said: fatal names.

units.la: Exitio crescent vestro, populiq; ruinisTollent caput superbum
units.tr: They will grow to your destruction, and by the ruin of the people they will raise their proud head.

units.la: O mala quanta ferent, audaces funera quantaGenti mouebunt francicæ!
units.tr: O what evils, what great deaths, these bold men will bring upon the French nation!

units.la: Non patriæ flammas, Helenem quæ duxit adulterDamnosiores intulit.
units.tr: They have brought upon the fatherland flames more ruinous than Helen, who led to adultery.

units.la: Non dedit Ausoniæ graviora incommoda dirusCarthaginensis Annibal.
units.tr: The dreadful Carthaginian Hannibal did not inflict harder troubles on Ausonia.

units.la: Hæc igitur memores prædicta revoluite, Galli,Quæ tristis euentus probat.
units.tr: Therefore, Gauls, remember these predictions and turn them over, which the sad outcome proves.

units.la: Et vestris tandem satiati cladibus, atqʒLuctu ruentis patriæ:
units.tr: And at last, sated with your own disasters and with grief for the falling fatherland:

units.la: Non fraude, ast Francùm vera virtute superbi,Malis carere quærite.
units.tr: Seek to be free of evils not by fraud but by true virtue, proud of the Franks.

units.la: Magnates veterum cretos de sanguine Regum, &Gallos fouete nobiles.
units.tr: Magnates born of the blood of ancient kings, and nobles, cherish the Gauls.

units.la: Gallos Gallus amat, pro Rege perire paratus,Pro chariore Patria.
units.tr: A Gaul loves Gauls, ready to die for the king, for the dearer fatherland.

units.la: Ad fines verum si spes deducet auaraVestros vagantes hospites,
units.tr: If greedy hope leads wandering strangers to your borders,

units.la: Excipere ignotos solita leuitate cauete,Cauete fraudes exteras.
units.tr: beware of receiving unknown men with your usual levity; beware of foreign frauds.

units.la: Indigenas Gallos nunquam hospes auarus ambit,Sibi suisq; proximus.
units.tr: A greedy stranger never seeks out the native Gauls, being close only to himself and his own.

units.la: Proditione, dolis, scelere, atqʒ libidine, & ira,Opes parabit impias. Hæc animis potior si stat sententia vestris,Vos vos labantes eriget.Sed quum aduersa trahāt Gallorum fata nepotes,Vana querela quid iuuant?
units.tr: By treachery, deceit, crime, lust and anger he will acquire impious wealth. If this opinion stands more firmly in your minds, it will raise you who are faltering. But since adverse fates drag the Gallic descendants, what good does vain complaint do?
Lectius's Reply.

units.tr: The verses that your candour, having read and reread them, dedicated to Condaeus and to me. Verses that bear witness to my nectar-sweet love, and that honour the hero with grief. Go on loving me, but put an end to your sorrow and exchange your mourning for joy. That he is alive, if you trust anything to a faithful friend, I announce that he is well. The rumour that falsely reported his death was, it seems, about to mock the cruel tyrants of its desired end. Rumour, which once was a harsh evil to great Maro, yet at last gives birth to some good. Whether the sparing Fate yielded to the pious bard, or, hating crime, gave back his life, whatever it was, it will never please you, Lectius, to assail such a report. The revered mystagogue who gave me this great pledge of great love would add to it.

units.tr: When rumour once troubled a father's anxious mind, announcing from far away that his beloved sons had fallen in a deadly war; or when, with cruel speech, it struck the breast of a virtuous, bright-faced wife, saying that her husband had perished in a ship whose timbers had come apart: that rumour, Lectius, which gave such news, will not quickly remove the great sorrow once it has changed, not even if it swears by the Supreme Deity that what it reported to itself was false. What if the father heard that his sons had come home in good health, or the faithful wife learned by true report that her husband had returned safe? Lest sleep deceive them with empty images, or a pleasant error mock them, they will foolishly take care, and though frightened they will scarcely be able to restore their minds. So I now refuse to believe you (I say that no one lives more truly than he) that the hero is well, as you announced to me in your welcome poem. But let a later rumour at last dispel the sad tidings of the earlier one, as the mournful verses are gladly and rightly sung again on a renewed plectrum.

From these parents there sprang a people, spread over all the habitable lands, wherever the bright sun shines over the wide world. units.tr: Bold in its youth and trusting in foreign strength, it cunningly sought to change sweet peace for civil war, and dared to dictate laws to the King of France. It drove him from his beloved cities, threatened slaughter and shameful chains, and ordered him, as he yielded to the harsh storms, to follow the standards of Lorraine. But the great mind of the King crushed their violence and their reckless assaults, and the better counsel of his foresight overcame their greater strength. Thus Pallas destroyed the Giants who threatened ruin to Jove, with her aegis, when she helped her father, who was hurling thunderbolts, with a better plan. The impious crowd gained nothing by its furious force, nor did Pelion piled upon Ossa. Force alone and its attempts always collapse under their own weight. Now that the treacherous enemies are overthrown, great King, shake off the troubled disturbances, and graciously restore lasting peace to the languishing homeland. For all Gaul, crushed by dire disasters, groans in every city, and the sorrowing, bloodied survivors of the slaughtered citizens repeat their lamentations.
Since Guise audaciously overturned the soft leisure of Francis,
and as the wicked author of civil war,
he violated the Frenchmen,
ferociously scorning the ordinances of the realm,
he, the prince, overthrew the royal edicts,
and, forcing the tender king along with his mother, alas, pitiably into arms,
with what fury he raged in his proud assault!
What great losses did he bring upon the Gauls!
What deadly disturbances has he caused among the French through the cities!
Thus when a fierce flood stirs up the quiet rivers, and the cattle and houses,
and wills to sweep away the roots together,
everything roars with terrible murmur.
Thus the cloudy Adriatic raises horrid storms with the restless south wind,
and the violent sea tosses the sailors wandering over the vast deep.
Thus the dread beast rages when hunger racks its belly, and in its fervent jaws,
angry, it slaughters the prey it has found, or the woolly flocks.
Hence the Gallic fields everywhere are soaked with poured-out blood,
The south-west wind raises dreadful storms,
And the sailors wandering across the vast
The violent wind lashes the sea.
So the dread beast rages when hunger
Wrings its belly, and with fiery tooth
Enraged, when it has found its prey,
Slaughters the woolly flocks.
Hence the Gallic fields everywhere
Are drenched with spilled blood, and the prey of savage beasts
Lie slain across the fields,
And the companies of the French lie dead.

units.la: Non urbs acerbis unica cerniturIntacta damnis, oppida turpibusQuassata bellis, civibusqueCuncta suis viduata lugent.
units.tr: No city is seen untouched by the cruel losses; the towns, shamefully battered by the wars, and all the cities, bereaved of their own citizens, mourn.

units.la: Non villa luctu mæsta caret domus.Plorat mariti funera tristiorConiux, & amisso tenellisPatre timet mala plura natis.
units.tr: No village or house is free from sorrowful grief. The wife weeps more sadly for her husband's death and fears further evils for her tender children, now that their father is lost.

units.la: Maternus, eheu! quæ dolor excitatLamenta, telis pectora quum videtTraiecta natorum, patérveQuum senior sepelit cruentos!
units.tr: Alas, what grief rouses laments when a mother sees her sons' breasts pierced by weapons, or when an aged father buries his bloodied children!

units.la: Quæ cuncta Gallis vulnera GallicusFecisse miles gestit acerbius,Francósque victos Francus audetEgregius spoliare victor!
units.tr: What wounds the French soldier eagerly and most bitterly inflicted on the Gauls! And the Frenchman, an outstanding victor, dares to despoil the conquered French!

units.la: Antiqua priscis temporibus fides,Virtúsque Francis subdita Regibus,Hostes remotos impetiitArma ferens metuenda cunctis:
units.tr: In former times the ancient faith and valour of the Franks were subject to their kings. Bearing arms feared by all, they attacked distant enemies.

units.la: Et signa iustis splendida LaureisLate per orbem Gallica protulit,Duxítque laudatos renidensBarbaricis opibus triumphos.
units.tr: And they carried far and wide the gleaming standards of Gaul with just laurels, and, rejoicing, they led triumphs celebrated for their barbarian wealth.

units.la: Sed nunc benignus te Superum fauor,Rex magne, nostris fletibus annuit,Plebes ut oppressas benignusTabifico releues labore
units.tr: But now, great King, the gracious favour of the gods nods to our tears, so that you, graciously, may relieve the people oppressed by wasting toil.

units.la: Vltor ligato fortior agmine, Gentísque tandem corda recolligas Diuísa, nec posthac redire Indigenas patiare motus. Nam veris instar vultus vbi tuus Plebi nitescet pacificus tua, Nubes serenata recedent, Præcipites fugient procellæ. Te Gallus hostes auspice Barbaros Iusto lacesset Marte potentior: Tuísque nunc damnis fruentes Vexet eques metuendus hasta. Impune captis vrbibus impotens Bellum Sabaudus mouerit impium Multísque quæsitas periclis Vsque tuas retinebit arces? Impune Gallis seditionibus Centaurus audax riserit Allobrox, Versámque Francorum superbis Contuderit pedibus coronam? Impune tectis proditionibus Fidens, & auro, cœperit otium Turbare Bernatum, & vetustis Fœderibus violare Gentes Gallis amicas? Tunde superbiam Tantósque fastus Principis exteri. Quis arma Francorum, tuísque Auspiciis sociata, rumpet? Sic dura cunctis sospes ab hostibus Sana ruentis vulnera patriæ: Compone civiles tumultus: Otia redde tuis cupita. Te rege tuti rura ferat labor Magnus coloni, per mare navita Currant quietum, Faustitáque Aurea sparget opes benignas. Vindex auaras destrue fortior Fraudes, vaganti frena licentiæ Repone, cædes & scelestas Pœna comes premat usque culpas. Sic regna magnis regibus obtine Rex maior, uno rite minor Deo. Sic laude venturi decorum Perpetua celebrent nepotes.
units.tr: Being stronger than an avenger with your army bound, you may at last gather together the hearts of the divided nation, and you will not allow the domestic disturbances to return again. For when your countenance shines upon the people like the spring, peaceful and yours, the clouds will recede, serene, and the headlong storms will flee. Under your auspices, the Frenchman, mightier in just war, will assail the enemies, the barbarians. And the horseman, feared with his spear, will harass those who now enjoy your losses. Will the Savoyard, powerless, ever raise impious war with impunity, after taking cities, and keep your citadels, won with many dangers, forever? Will the bold Allobrogian centaur laugh with impunity at the seditions of the Gauls, and crush the crown of the French, turned, beneath his proud feet? Will Bernatus, trusting in roofs of treachery and in gold, dare with impunity to disturb the peace and violate the ancient covenants with the nations friendly to the Gauls? Crush the pride and the haughty arrogance of the foreign prince. Who will break the arms of the Franks, allied under your auspices? Thus, safe from the hostile enemies, heal the deep wounds of the collapsing homeland. Calm the civil tumults. Restore to your people the leisure they desire. Under your rule may great labour bring the fields to the farmer, and may the sailor run over the sea in peace, and may golden Fortune scatter her gracious riches. As avenger, more strongly destroy greedy frauds, restore the reins to wandering licence, and let punishment, as companion, always press down wicked crimes. Thus rule the kingdoms, greater king, lesser only in right, to one God. Thus may the coming descendants, in praise, forever celebrate what is fitting.
To the same man.

units.la: Sic te Cœlituum pater Cunctis incolumem seruet ab hostibus, Et nostris precibus fauens Pergat sacrilegæ gentis, & hospitæ, Luratas caput in tuum Dextras fulmineo rumpere brachio: Vt rex sceptra rebellibus Tandem perdomitis Gallica temperans Pacis dulcia CandidaPlebi restituat otia subdita.
units.tr: So may the Father of the heavenly ones keep you safe from all enemies. Favouring our prayers, may he go on to break with his thunderbolt-arm the sworn right hands raised against your head by a sacrilegious and foreign race, so that the king, at last having subdued the rebels and governing French affairs with moderation, may restore sweet peace and quiet to the loyal commons who are subject to him.

units.la: Audax Guisiadum genusDeceptum magicis cantibus, & sibiFrancum debita somniansRegna, & pollicitis excitum fbericisTerra misfcuit æthera.Produxit q, suis seditionibusBelli iurgia ciuici,Et Gallos variis cladibus obruit.
units.tr: The bold race of the Guises, deceived by magic songs and dreaming of the kingdom they claim as their own and of France, roused by Spanish promises, has mingled earth with heaven. It has also, by its seditions, brought on the quarrels of civil war, and has overwhelmed the French with various disasters.

units.la: Audax Gens LotharingicaDumse Pontificum relligionibusAddictam magis omnibusFingit, dum veteres, quas vocat, hæresesArdet perdere funditus,O quàm multiplices cauta reconditisTexit pectoribus dolos,Fraudes, insidias, perfidiam & scelus,Regi perniciem suo,Gallis seruitium turpius apparans.
units.tr: The bold Lorraine race, while it pretends to be more devoted than all others to the religion of the Pontiffs, while it burns to destroy utterly what it calls the old heresies, has woven, O how many-fold, the cunning deceits hidden in its breasts: frauds, plots, treachery and crime, preparing ruin for its king and a more shameful slavery for the French.

units.la: Sed qui sceptra Deus tibi,Rex Henrice, dedit Gallica flectere,Hic mentis quoque prouidæIunctum Consilium viribus addidit.Sic nunc lethiferam cauesGentis perfidiam fortior impiæ.Sic regnum tibi traditumIamiam propitio Numine vindicas.
units.tr: But God, who gave you, King Henry, the sceptres of France to bend, has added to your mind's foresight a counsel joined with strength. So now you guard against the deadly treachery of that impious race more boldly. Thus, already, by the favour of the Divine power, you vindicate the kingdom handed down to you.

units.la: Sic spes Guisiadum vagas,Optatamque tua morte TyrannidemVictor splendidus obteris,Et tristi patriam funere liberas.Heu! mens caca cupidineQuum regni rapitur, quo ruit impetuPraeceps per vetitum nefas?Nullum turpe putat flagitium, aut scelus,Leges iuraque negligit,Caelesti arbitrio cuncta negans regi.Nullos illa deos, nequePlectendis metuit Tartara sontibus.Fertur filia mortuumConculcasse ferox Tullia ServiumBigis, dum properat patrisRegem cade sui cernere coniugem.Regno fraudibus impiisDavidem pepulit filius Absalom.Quem mox dextera NuminisFeriens aetherei perdidit exituTristi, qui manet improbosConatus meritum supplicium ferens.
units.tr: Thus, gloriously victorious, you crush the wandering hopes of the Guises and the tyranny they hoped to win by your death, and you free the fatherland from grievous mourning. Alas, when a mind blinded by greed is seized by lust for a kingdom, where does it rush headlong through forbidden wickedness? It thinks no disgrace or crime shameful, neglects laws and rights, and denies everything to the heavenly judgment of the king. It fears no gods, nor Tartarus where the guilty are punished. It is said that the fierce Tullia drove her chariot over the dead body of Servius, hurrying to see her husband made king by her father's slaughter. By impious frauds, the son Absalom drove David from the kingdom. Soon the right hand of the Deity, striking him, destroyed him with a sad heavenly end, which awaits wicked attempts and bears the punishment they deserve.
TO HENRY III, KING OF NAVARRE.

units.la: ANTIQVA Regum progenies, decus Illustre Gentis Borbonicæ, cui Lucescit inter clariores Conspicuum caput vsque Gallos: Quo te celebrem carmine? qua Lyra Dicam benigni robora pectoris Inuicta? quo iusti tenacem Proposití resonare tentem Heroa plectro: quem popularium Non terret ardor praua iubentium, Iraeque Magnatum, nec arma Sanguinea sociata turbæ? Quem non profanis, quæ rotat arcibus Romanus atrox fulmina Pontifex, Nec feruor instantis pericli Mente quatit solida pauentem? Immota rupes sic manet ictibus Vtcunque raucis vnda furens petat: Quum miscet insanis patentem Æolus Oceanum procellis. Milesne tantum perdere principem
units.tr: Ancient offspring of kings, illustrious glory of the Bourbon race, whose conspicuous head shines above the most famous of the Gauls: with what song shall I celebrate you? With what lyre shall I tell of the unconquered strength of your generous heart? With what plectrum shall I try to sing of the hero, steadfast in his resolve to be just, whom neither the fierce passion of the common people, commanding base things, nor the anger of the great men terrifies, nor arms joined with a bloodthirsty mob? Whom the thunderbolts that the Roman Pontiff, fierce and profane, hurls from his citadels do not shake, nor does the heat of imminent peril move his steadfast mind? Thus the rock stays unmoved against blows, however hoarsely the raging wave beats upon it, when Aeolus stirs the open ocean with mad storms. Did the Gaul dare, alas, under a barbarous leader, to attempt the ruin of so great a prince?

units.la: Tentauit, eheu! sub duce Barbaro Gallus? Tyrannorumque signa Hospita Guisiadum sequutus Funesta Gallis praelia cinibus Impune mouit? Ruraque feruido Sulcata Francorum labore Marte suo populata vidit? Quum sceptra Genti Gallica perfida, Et fraudulento prodidit hospiti: Quum iussa vellet subiugatos Francigenas Lotharinga ferre? Tali superbis milite, Guisie, Regnumque poscis, quidlibet impotens Sperare, per vastas ruentis Dum patriae furit ille cades. Sic regna Stirpi debita regiae Galloque captas aduena principi? Sic prisca Legum sacra turbas Et Salicae pia iura Normae? Te blandienti somnus imagine, Te mentis error ludit amabilis: Quum sceptra Gallorum lacertis Grandia non paribus prehensas. Qui regna terris diuidit omnibus, Qui regna firmat legibus additis Tremendus author, Gentibusque Iura dedit, violanda nulli: Qui cuncta rubri fulminis ignibus
units.tr: Did the Gaul, following the hospitable banners of the tyrant Guises, stir up deadly wars against the Gauls and their own ashes with impunity? Did he see the country fields, furrowed by the labour of the Franks, ravaged by his own Mars? When the treacherous Gallic nation surrendered its sceptres and betrayed them to a deceitful guest, when Lorraine wished to impose the orders of the subjugated Franks: with such a soldier, proud Guise, you demand the kingdom, powerless to hope for anything at all, while that man rages through the vast slaughters of his falling country. Thus does a stranger seize kingdoms owed to the royal stock and captured by the Gallic prince? Thus do you disturb the sacred ancient laws and the pious rights of the Salic law? Sleep, with its flattering image, mocks you; a lovable error of the mind deceives you, when you have seized the great sceptres of the Gauls with arms not equal to them. He who divides kingdoms among all lands, who strengthens kingdoms by the laws he adds, the awesome author, who gave laws to the nations that no one may violate, who with the fires of a red thunderbolt

units.la: Terret caducis, quum ferit arduusTitanus Ætneos, minásqueCentimanas cohibet Gigantum:
units.tr: terrifies all that is frail, as the lofty Titan strikes Mount Etna and restrains the threatening hundred-handed giants.

units.la: Te perduelli cum grege turpiumPerdet virorum, Barbare, GallicæFatalis monstrum Gentis, atqueInnocuo rutilans cruore
units.tr: You, Barbarian, with a band of disloyal men, the fatal monster of the Gallic nation, destroys, glowing with innocent blood.

units.la: Immanis, ehen! belIua, quæ bonosSummi sequentes dogmata NuminisVirgis cruentas, ine torres,Et crucibus lacerásque ferro.
units.tr: Monstrous, alas, beast of war, who torture the good who follow the doctrines of the highest God with bloody rods, and tear them with crosses and iron.

units.la: Verùm retectis Guisiadum dolis,Quæ nunc Nauarrum Gallia principemVirtute sublimi decorumMarte ferox petit impotente,
units.tr: But now the tricks of the Guises are exposed, and Gaul, fierce with impotent war, seeks to destroy the prince of Navarre, adorned with sublime virtue.

units.la: Tandem secundo Numine sospitem,Pacata, iustis reddet honoribus,Et proximis regi benignaSedibus egregium reponet.
units.tr: At last, saved by a second divine favour, Gaul, pacified, will restore him with just honours, and kindly place him, distinguished, in the seats nearest the king.

units.la: Quem nunc cruentis fraudibus explicat,Et præparatis mortibus eximit,Cunctisque seruatum periclisIncolumem fovet aduocataChristi potentis dextera vindicis.
units.tr: Whom now she frees from bloody frauds and rescues from prepared deaths, and keeps him unharmed amid all dangers, cherished by the powerful right hand of Christ the avenger, who is his advocate.

units.la: Hæc sola vires subruit impias.Hæc tela coniurata rumpitSacrilegæ potior caterua,
units.tr: This alone overthrows impious forces. This breaks the weapons of the sacrilegious band that has conspired against him.
By this he, trusting, guards himself against the poisons (of the subtle
hidden snares of the people) guards against.
By this he, secure, has often broken
the fierce threats and the swords
when the fury, with its cruel prelate as author,
did not before loosen the reins of licence
with burning zeal through the cities,
when the fierce butchery, ranging through the French,
insolently terrified the peoples.
When the crowd, conscious of the true God,
unwary and dreadfully deceived by treacherous
fraud, is struck down, its peace slain,
and the sacred breasts entrusted to Christ
were slaughtered by the savage hand of the butchers
everywhere, nor sparing the unwarlike youth,
the virgins and boys.
When Gaul, with a mournful trumpet call,
frenzied, tore apart its own citizens,
and with innocent blood poured out
polluted all the cities.
Thus the Maenads who celebrate the rites of Bacchus
rage fiercely when the drums clash.
Thus Agave, glad at the ruin of her own,
the mother, slaughters Pentheus.
But the kindly favour of the gods
through weapons and enemies, best of princes,
has saved you, snatched from the raging ones,
and will bring perpetual help.
Because you duly honour the Divinity with true honours,

units.la: Votisque semper supplicibus colis,Quod inssa seruas, & potentiTegeris vsque Deo minorem.Quid tuta virtus praesidio PatrisPossit supremi, quid queat indolesAddicta Christo, PrincipisqueQuid valeant pia vota iustiHostilis ardens agminis impetusSensit retusus nuper, & aemulaeSensere, quae tristi cohortesCortracia cecidere pugna:Sensitq; Ductor, funera qui tibiAudax parabat dura Iovesivs:Quum vota risisset piorumSollicitasque preces superbus.Nam victa spreto Numine brachiisFidens iuventus cum Duce corruit:Vicitque caelestem precatusMiles opem metuendus hosti.Sic praepotenti Iessaides precePugnauit olim, quum rudis agminumFudit Philistaeas phalanges,Atque trucem feriit Gigantem:Quem mole vasta corporis arduiArmabat ensis, cuspis & aneaIngentis hastae: cuique pectusAere ferox solido micabat.Hic fastuoso lumine militem
units.tr: Always worshipping with suppliant vows, because you keep his commands and, though you are a lesser man, are sheltered by the mighty God. What can safe virtue do under the protection of the supreme Father; what can a youth devoted to Christ do, and what can the pious prayers of a just prince avail? The hostile army's fierce onslaught felt it, recently repulsed, and the rivals felt it, the cohorts that fell in the sad battle; and the leader felt it, who was daring enough to prepare death for you by harsh Jove's decree, when he proudly laughed at the vows of the pious and their anxious prayers. For the youth, trusting in arms and scorning the Divinity, fell with their leader; but the soldier, feared by the enemy, conquered after praying for heavenly help. Thus once the son of Jesse fought with powerful prayer, when he routed the Philistine phalanxes of the untrained armies and struck down the fierce giant, whom the vast bulk of his body, a sword, and a bronze spear-point of huge size armed; whose breast glittered fiercely with solid bronze. Seeing the little soldier, he scorned him with a haughty look.

units.la: Cernens pusillum, spreuit, & impotensIrae tumentis, dira saeuisVocibus atq; cruces minatusIntentat hastam: sed Dauid occupat,Fundaq; paruo vulnere stupeaeMagnum Gigantem funeratumExuuiis spoliat superbis.
units.tr: And, unrestrained by swelling anger, threatening with savage words, he hurls his spear; but David, anticipating him with a stone from a sling, struck the great giant with a small wound, and, when he had fallen dead, stripped him of his proud spoils.

units.la: Sed plura molli dicere barbitoVetat tenella Musa potens Lyrae,Quae gestit heroas CothurnoMaeoniy resonare vatis.
units.tr: But the tender Muse, powerful in the lyre, forbids me to say more on the soft barbitos; she longs to sing of heroes in the buskin of the Maeonian bard.

units.la: EADEM DIE DVX GVI-SIVS INTERFECTVS QVA Rex Nauarrae natus.
units.tr: The same day the Duke of Guise was killed, on which the King of Navarre was born.

units.la: VAE te nascentem, Rex, magni conscia partusOstendit terris, prima, Nauarre dies,Guisiadem ad stygias iussit penetrare paludes,Auctior ut duplici luce at usque nota.Nam te praesidium patriae dedit illa ruentiHic semper cuius pestis acerba fuit.
units.tr: Woe to you, King, when the first day of your birth, Navarre, conscious of a great delivery, showed you to the lands, and ordered Guise to penetrate the Stygian marshes, so that you might be more glorious in the double light that was always known. For that day gave you as a protection to your country, you who were rushing upon that one whose bitter plague had always been here.
ANOTHER.

units.la: ILLA dies terris quæ te tulit ante, Navarre,Ut columen patriæ conspicerétve patrem,Indignata tibi crudelia fata parareGuisiadem, hunc subito frigore iusta ferit,Vnius ardentes restinguens sanguine flammas,Gallorumq; vna plurima bella nece.Clara dies tanti regis natalibus, EugeClarior adscito funere Guisiadæ.
units.tr: That day which bore you to the earth before, Navarre, so that you might behold the pillar and the father of your country, and which, indignant that cruel fates were being prepared for you, strikes Guise suddenly with a just chill, quenching the burning flames with the blood of one man, and with the one slaughter of Guise ending very many wars of the Gauls. A bright day for the birthdays of so great a king, brighter still by the death of Guise, which was brought about.
ANOTHER.

units.la: Quæ te (Rex) terris ostendit prima, NavarreSignetur creta nobiliore diesNascentis nam fausta prius cunabula vitæQuum dedit, hoc dixit non satis esse tibi,Ni te perpetuo comitetur amica fauore,Atq; hostes cunctos perdat acerba tuos.Hoc facit, unius lethæo flumine mersumGuisiadis tandem quum rapit illa caput.
units.tr: The first day that showed you to the earth, Navarre, king, let it be marked with whiter chalk, for when it gave you a fortunate cradle of your early life, it said that this was not enough for you unless a friendly favour should accompany you perpetually and bitterly destroy all your enemies. It does this, when at last it snatches the head of Guise, plunged into the Lethean stream of one man.
THE EFFECTS OF THE GUISE'S PUNISHMENT.
Since the mightier Fate has lately slain him, struggling
The Guisiad, and ordered him to approach the Stygian lakes:
France hoped for peace by his death,
He who was the author of the wretched sedition.

units.la: Spes breuis illa fuit. Ciuis nam pallidus Orci
units.tr: That hope was brief. For the pale citizen of Orcus
now stirs all Acheron together with the Furies.
ANOTHER.
With the Guise extinguished, why does all France renew
the greater tumults, and rage more savagely?

units.la: O demum infelix nunc Gallia, terque quaterque!
units.tr: O France, now at last unhappy, thrice and four times!
By this death quiet ought to have returned to you.
ANOTHER.
Because the King destroyed the Guisiads by a violent death,

units.la: Vt vita, vt regno consuleret, que suo:
units.tr: to provide for his life and for his kingdom, which were his own:
now squalid France pours forth sad tears,
and wages treacherous wars on him everywhere.
Shameful tears! shameful wars! what can be more foul than these
tears and arms?
Does it grieve the Guisiads' schemes that he has escaped them?
Would it be wished that this was not permitted to the King his own?
Against the Duke of Mayenne.

units.la: Quo se iure putat Dux Gallis iura daturum Mænius, & Valesis sceptra tributa petit?
units.tr: By what right does Mayenne think he will give laws to the French, and seek the sceptres due to the Valois?

units.la: Cur validas armat per Gallica rura cohortes?
units.tr: Why does he arm strong cohorts across the French countryside?

units.la: Cur Gallos cogit iam sua iussa sequi?
units.tr: Why does he now force the French to follow his commands?

units.la: Huic mater, Veneris recludens furta, parente Regius es, dixit, sanguis utroque puer.
units.tr: His mother, revealing the intrigues of Venus, said to him: "You are a child of royal blood on both sides, born of a royal parent."

units.la: Nunc Regi non est, mihi crede, propinquior alter.
units.tr: Now, believe me, no one else is nearer to the King.
Gossip calls you, wrongly, a son of the Guises.

units.la: Aude ergo, ut quondam Macedo, quum matre monente Se genitum Ammonio credidit esse Ioue.
units.tr: Dare then, as the Macedonian once did, when his mother advised him and he believed himself begotten by Jupiter Ammon.

units.la: AD CLARISS. VIRVM D. Th. BEZAM CARMEN.
units.tr: TO THE DISTINGUISHED MAN D. Th. BEZA, A POEM.

units.la: INFANS, quum patrias Beza tenellus Vagitu insolito concuteret domos, Miratúsque nouam, non sine Numine, Lucem cerneret acrior:
units.tr: INFANT Beza, while still tender, shook his native home with unaccustomed cries, and, marvelling at the new light, looked about with keen eyes, not without the will of God.

units.la: Illum Pierides, & Charitum chorus, Illum cum Clario Pallas Apolline Viderunt faciles: vidit & addita Cunctis laeta Lubentia.
units.tr: The Pierides and the chorus of the Graces saw him, and gentle Pallas with Clarian Apollo; and joyful Lubentia, added to them all, saw him too.

units.la: Montisque vnanimes verticibus sacris Conuenêre sui: qua strepit vngula Fons reclusus equi limpidus alitis: Qua Lauri virides comas Spargunt, Phoebigenûm praemia frontium.
units.tr: The Muses, of one mind, gathered to their sacred mountain peaks, where the spring opened by the hoof of the winged horse babbles clear, and where they scatter green laurel leaves, the rewards of brows born of Phoebus.

units.la: Atque umbras gracilès consiliantibus Dant Musis. Pueri Cynthius Indolem Princeps laudibus extulit.
units.tr: And they gave slender shades to the counselling Muses. The Cynthian prince praised the boy's promise with praise.

units.la: Hunc carmen citharaiußit Eburnea Maiorem reliquis reddere vatibus.
units.tr: The ivory lyre commanded this song to make him greater than the other poets.

units.la: Hunc Lauri voluit tollere pluribus Ornatum foliis caput.
units.tr: The laurel wished to lift his head, adorned with more leaves.
The Castalides together welcome the words of their brother
with happy applause, and with new gifts
they enrich the Delphic gifts:
nor do they deny the boy anything.
But Pallas, kinder than usual of her own accord,
adorns him with special honours,
while she waters his lively lips
with the flowing juices of eloquence;
and hidden Wisdom, as his companion,
led him by an unknown way up the steep
hills, so that she might tinge his generous breast
there with the choicest colours.
The Graces, whom placid Lubentia, joined to them, always
brightens with her honeyed bosom, pouring out
delights; and Grace herself, and the flowing charm of grace,
flutter around them.
With these as guides, Beza at once, his side scorning the ground,
and with wings that do not tremble,
turned into a purple bird,
cuts through the immense air.
If it pleases him to contend with the Aeolian lyres
among the lovely choirs of poets,
Delius nods that he, the victor, shall gather
the famous laurels.
To him yield the inhabitants of the Teutonic border,
the drinker of the Eridanus, and the Italian;
and those whom Gaul, richer in its milky udder,
nourishes as poets.

units.la: Verùm perpetua si Sapientiæ Facundo reserat iura recondita Ore, & si placidis cœtibus indicat Qua cœlum petitur via:
units.tr: But if with eloquent mouth she unlocks the hidden laws of perpetual Wisdom, and if she shows to peaceful assemblies the way by which heaven is sought:

units.la: Illi mella, fluunt æmula nectari, Sacro digna sonat ritè silentio, Et quæ vulgus amat, turbáq; doctior Intentis bibit auribus.
units.tr: honey flows for him, rivalling nectar; he sounds worthy of sacred silence; and the crowd, made more learned, drinks in with attentive ears what the common people love.

units.la: Sic mirata suum Græcia Nestorem Olim densa humeris dulciloquum audiit: Quum verba eximiis picta leporibus Cano pectore promeret.
