units.tr: Thus Greece once marvelled at her Nestor, and heard him, sweet-speaking, with broad shoulders, when he brought forth words painted with choice charms from a grey heart.

units.la: Sic mirata frequens audiit Herculem Prisci's temporibus Gallia Celticum, Aures quum domitas duceret aureis Victrix lingua catenulis.
units.tr: Thus Gaul, in ancient times, marvelled at and gladly heard the Celtic Hercules, when his victorious tongue led ears tamed with golden chains.

units.la: Sic Musis niteas Bezafauentibus Semper conspicuo vertice clarior, Et nomen meritis laudibus inclitum Cunctis Gentibus inferas.
units.tr: Thus, Beza, may you shine ever brighter in the eyes of the Muses with a conspicuous crown, and carry your name, renowned for its merits and praises, to all nations.

units.la: Maiorem invidia te petat Invidus, Ceu Cygnum obstreperis vocibus anseres, Et ceu quum rabidis Lunam vlulatibus Nocturnus canis impetit.
units.tr: May the envious man, with envy, seek you the more, as geese with their raucous voices assail a swan, and as a night dog attacks the moon with rabid howling.
A GIFT OF A CUP, TO THE SAME.

units.la: DOctarum potis ElegantiarumBeza magnificas referre laudes,Pocillum artificis sagacioreMitto Dædalei manu politum:Vicinio tui fauente torno.Quod vix excipiat cauo pusilloFlentis lachrymulam unicam puelli.Quod vix ventriculo queat minutoRoris exiguam tenere guttam.Quo formica suam labore fessaIugi paruula vix sitim leuarit.Quo nec florilega sagax proboscisMergi possit apis calente sole:Nec arguta semel cicada siccasCantu perpetuo rigare fauces.Vix illo valeat culex iacere,Aut pulex tenuis latere totus.O si tam modicis, minutulisquePauxillo madidis mero cululisDecertare modo iuuaret acresPotores: neque poculo liceretProuocare viros capaciore!Laudarent Sapido politioresVates Teutonici suos: nec vnquamTam charis biberent merum popinis.
units.tr: Since I am able, Beza, to report the magnificent praises of learned elegance, I send you a little cup, polished by the hand of a craftsman more skilful than Daedalus, with the neighbouring lathe favouring your work: a cup that scarcely holds the single tear of a weeping little boy, that scarcely keeps a tiny drop of dew in its small belly, into which a thirsty ant, worn out by labour, could scarcely relieve its constant thirst in the sun, nor could a wise bee dip its flower-gathering proboscis, nor a shrill cicada ever wet its dry throat with unending song. A gnat could scarcely lie in it, or a slender flea hide wholly in it. Oh, if only such tiny, little cups, soaked with a pinch of wine, could contend with keen drinkers, and it were allowed to challenge men with a larger cup! The more refined German poets would praise their own sweet wine, and they would never drink in such dear taverns.
To Petrus Poppaeus, the poet.

units.la: {ASCIVA Musa cantica virgines Odere, blandas delicias Lyræ Arcent profanæ, non Poetam Pierij patiuntur antri Sacris adesse, & tollere Delphicas Æterna Lauros præmia, si probat Obscœnus incestos amores, Furta docens Veneris nefanda. Sunt hæc canoræ murmura tibiæ, Poppæe, Musis dulcia, Numinis Quæ facta supremi recensent, Vtque suum moderatur orbem, Seu sævientes sacrilega manu Cogat Gigantes regna Proserpinæ Vmbrasque pallentes adire, Fulminea metuendus arce: Seu copioso munere largior Fœcundat agros, lætáque pascuis Armenta nutrit, pacibúsque Agricolas recreat quietis. Sunt digna Phœbo, sunt Chariúm choris Iucunda, vates carmina quæ pius
units.tr: The Muse, unwilling to sing hymns, shuns the pleasing delights of the lyre. The profane keep it away, and the Pierian cave's poet does not allow it to attend the sacred rites or to take the Delphic laurels, eternal prizes, if the obscene poet approves of incestuous loves, teaching the unspeakable thefts of Venus. These are the sweet murmurs of the tuneful flute, Poppaeus, sweet to the Muses, which recount the deeds of the supreme Deity and how he governs his world: whether, with a sacrilegious hand, he forces the Giants to approach the kingdom of Proserpina and the pale shades, he who is to be feared, thundering from his citadel; or whether, more generous with abundant gifts, he makes the fields fruitful, nourishes the herds in the pastures, and refreshes the farmers with the peace of quiet. Such songs are worthy of Phoebus and pleasing to the dances of the Graces, which the pious poet sings

units.la: Castúsque Musarum sacerdosVirginibus puerisque cantat:Pulchris tenellas qui studiis valetFormare mentes, qui simul arduaVirtutis occultum recludensMonstrat iter venerandus author.
units.tr: and the chaste priest of the Muses sings to virgins and boys, he who can shape tender minds with fine studies, who at the same time unlocks the hidden path of virtue and shows the way, the venerable author.

units.la: Qui damna mollis pellit inertia,Prauúmque frenat ritè Cupidinem:Duros iuuentus vt laboresPro patria tolerare discat:Qui sancta fidos foedera coniugesSeruare cogit, commoda seu thoriLaudat fidelis seu pudorisIura sacri violata damnat:Qui facta non fert inclita fortiumObliuiones carpere limidas,Chartísve inornatos sileriEgregios pietate Reges.
units.tr: He who drives away the losses of soft idleness and rightly curbs wicked Cupid, so that youth may learn to endure hard labours for the fatherland; who compels faithful spouses to keep their holy covenant, who praises the benefits of marriage or condemns the violated rights of faithful chastity; who does not suffer the famous deeds of brave men to be picked apart by timid forgetfulness, nor allows the distinguished kings renowned for piety to be passed over in unadorned pages.

units.la: Nam cum vaganti frena licentiaPonunt, pudendum cum scelus obruuntCulpásque conantur nocentesVindicibus remouere poenis,Fulgens nitenti vertice FaustitasIllustrat vrbes, rura Ceres beat,Et larga cornu plenioreCopia fundit opes benignas.
units.tr: For when they put a rein on wandering licence, cover over shameful crime, and strive to remove guilty faults by avenging punishments, Prosperity, shining with a bright brow, lights up the cities, Ceres blesses the fields, and Abundance, with her horn fuller still, pours out her bountiful riches.

units.la: Hanc perge dulci materiem LyraeAptare, vastos ætheris vt petas
units.tr: Go on to fit this material to the sweet lyre, so that you may seek the vast regions of the sky

units.la: POPPÆ tractus, cui virescet Aonia caput usque fronde.
units.tr: of Poppaeus, whose head will flourish with Aonian foliage forever.
In praise of spectacles.
He has deserved the everlasting honour of praise,
who first set the twin swaying orbs of glass
master of an exquisite art,
bade them gleam upon swollen noses,
hanging, new little eyes of glass,
like twin torches and twin suns,
or as with splendid flames to cheer
dim, shadowed eyes,
aged and at once watery-eyed,
as the learned one: when sight, blunted by old age, grows dull,
when the tender pupil grows numb,
weakened by the infirmity of sickness.
Those more skilled in the medical art,
Machaon and his brother Podalirius,
and their parent Chiron himself,
who in the times of an earlier age dared
to teach the various powers of herbs
and eye-salves for protecting the light,
knew nothing of the sight of gleaming glass.
This one restrains the scattered fires of the eye,
revives the extinguished, and with a new and hidden
vigour quickens the drowsy senses,

units.la: Et longo recreat labore fessos. Vitreis oculis novis gemellis Gemelli iuvenum vigent ocelli, Gemellique senum vident ocelli.
units.tr: and refreshes the weary after long labour. With new twin glass eyes, the twin eyes of young men flourish, and the twin eyes of old men see.

units.la: Nunc vos luminibus meis misellis Certam fertis opem benigniora Vestris lucidulis specilla flammis. Sic Phoebi, Charitum, & novem sororum Interesse mihi licet Choreis. Sic clara licet eruditione Semper volvere nobiles libellos.
units.tr: Now bring to my poor eyes a surer help, kinder than your bright flames, spectacles. Thus may I be present at the dances of Phoebus, the Graces, and the nine sisters. Thus, famous for my learning, may I always turn over noble books.
On the Gnat Enclosed in a Globule

units.la: Succino, sive Electro incluso, CARMEN, Ad Ioannem Baptistam Rothanum, in Ecclesia Genevensi verbi Dei ministrum.
units.tr: Poem on a Gnat Enclosed in Amber, To John Baptist Rothanus, minister of the Word of God in the Genevan Church.

units.la: Si tecum mihi nunc licet iocari, Et nugas dare nobiles amico, Salsque innocuos, facetiasque: Defunctli Culicis, Rothane, Manes Mitto pallidulos, minutulosque. Rides? Limpidula videre fas est Iamiam (ni tibi lippiant ocelli) Illos molliter urnula iacentes:
units.tr: If I may now jest with you, and give trifles to a noble friend, and harmless salt and pleasantries: I send you, Rothanus, the pale and tiny shades of a dead gnat. You laugh? Unless your eyes are blurred, you may soon see those clear little things lying softly in the small urn.

units.la: Annosam nec opus tibi Sibillam Aureos prius indicare ramos: Nec tentare Magi furentis artes, Vt cernas Erebi latentis antro Vmbras lucidulis volare pennis. Hîc non Phidiaca manu toreuma Caelatum nitet, aut imago ludit, Qualem vel speculi remittit aequor, Vel fingit placida quiete somnus, Vel pictor varia figurat arte. Hîc non illicitis manere iussus Pithon carminibus struit dolosas Sortes, Tartareóve fallit astu. Hîc veri Culicis nitente gemma Veras reliquias vides sepultas, Qui quondam Heliadum fluente rore Vnáque implicitus repente gutta, Viscoso riguit gelu peremptus.
units.tr: You need no aged Sibyl to show you first the golden boughs, nor to attempt the arts of a raging magician, so that you might see, in the cave of hidden Erebus, shadows flying on bright wings. Here no carved toreutic work gleams from a Phidian hand, nor does any image play, such as the surface of a mirror gives back, or sleep feigns in placid quiet, or a painter shapes with varied skill. Here Python, bidden to stay, does not build deceptive oracles with forbidden incantations, nor deceive with Tartarean cunning. Here, in the shining gem of the true gnat, you see its true remains buried: the gnat that once, caught suddenly by a single drop of the flowing dew of the Heliades, stiffened, destroyed by viscous ice.

units.la: Huius magna Themis necem cruentam Et casus subitos miserta iussit, Vt quae lachryma sanior necarat Illi perpetuum foret sepulchrum: Quale non Phariys vetusta fecit Ægyptus Ducibus: vel ipsa charis Artemisia manibus mariti: Cedat Pyramidum labor superbus, Et quae splendida nunc premunt sepultos Reges marmora: quos nefas videre, Quos tempus, caries, situsque perdit: Quos nec balsama vindicant odora, Nec seruant Alabastra fœta Nardo, Nec quod mittit Arabs & Indus vnguen. Sed totus patet hoc Culex sepulchro Auri splendidius micante lamna: Cui nec dente potest nocere tristi Tempus, nec caries, situsve turpis. Tam belle Culici queunt sepulto Reges, si licet, inuidere tantum.
units.tr: Great Themis, pitying its bloody death and sudden fall, ordered that the tear which had killed it, being the more wholesome, should become its perpetual tomb. Such a tomb the ancient Egyptians did not make for their leaders, the Pharaohs, nor Artemisia for her dear husband. Let the proud labour of the pyramids give way, and the splendid marbles that now press down buried kings, whom it is unlawful to see, whom time, decay and squalor destroy, whom fragrant balsams do not protect, nor alabaster jars full of nard preserve, nor the unguent sent by the Arab and the Indian. But this gnat lies wholly visible in a tomb that gleams more brightly than gold plate. Neither time with its gnawing tooth, nor decay, nor foul squalor can harm it. So finely could kings, if it were allowed, only envy the buried gnat.
ON POETS. TO GUILLAUME MOGNÆUS.

units.la: NOn, si quid Latio ludere pectine Concessit facilis Pegasidum chorus Me Gallis cupidum vatibus inserit, Et Lauros patitur tollere duplices: Ceu, Mognæe, putas. Lancibus impares Phœbus spargit opes imparibus suas. Sunt qui Mæonij carminis alite Heroum celebrant facta potentium, Et magni altiloquas Virgilij tubas Inflant non pauidi, belláque differunt? Et Martem tunica tectum adamantina. Verùm hic mœsta canit, tristibus indicans
units.tr: If, Mognæus, you think that the easy band of the Pegasides has allowed me, playing with the plectrum in Latium, to join the Gallic poets who desire it, and has permitted me to lift up the double laurels, you are mistaken. Phoebus scatters his riches unequally on unequal dishes. There are those who, on the wing of the Maeonian song, celebrate the deeds of mighty heroes, and, not fearful, blow the lofty trumpets of great Virgil, and wage wars, and Mars covered in adamantine armour. But here I sing sorrowful things, declaring in elegies the human anxieties with sad strains,
Human anxieties in elegies,
And the headlong flights of fragile life
He sings more clearly in a plaintive song.
To him the Muse gave the power to pierce
With a biting sharpness the vice lying hidden in the hearts
And to castigate with witty jests and salt
The corrupt morals of men who follow depraved ways,
And the ruin of wandering licence.
And if Phoebus looks upon someone with a placid light,
He gives the nectar-sweet glory of the Cithara
Of the pleasing lyre, with which the solemn Stesichorus sang,
And the threatening Alcaeus, and the Rhodopeian
Orpheus; which Anacreon with an easy thumb
Struck, sounding of tender loves.
Which once he brought to Latin ears.
The chief Flaccus, pleasing, led the Aeolian song
Into Italian measures.
There are those who write songs in Greek-born voices;
but others soothe the sons of Romulus
with Ausonian sounds, and the Muse gives
to the Gallic poets the native pipe to play.
To a few she sends those gifts together, more generous,
If the three Graces favour,
And Phoebus the father nods his assent to the Cithara.
So Beza bids his threefold laurels be borne,
so he adorns him with various honours,
the learned one to play upon the Cecropian plectrum,

units.la: Doctum Romuleo pangere barbito. Et doctum fidibus dicere Gallicis:Quæ non liuor edax, nec mora temporum,Saturnúsve truci falce potens metet.
units.tr: the learned one to compose on the Romulean barbitos, and the learned one to speak with Gallic lyres, which neither devouring envy, nor the delay of time, nor Saturn, powerful with his cruel sickle, will reap.

units.la: IOANNI DVRANTIO GALLO REGIORVM ÆDIFICIORUM QUÆSTORI.
units.tr: TO JOHN DURANTIUS, A FRENCHMAN, QUAESTOR OF THE ROYAL BUILDINGS.

units.la: HEu, Chiragra, malum ferox, furénsque,Furui filia Tartari, miserellosQuæ diris, Stygijs, feris, tremendisMortales cruciatibus fatigas,Nostro parce, precor, precor Duranto:Parce, nec manibus nocere fas sitCentum, quas colit, artium peritis,Et centum simul elegantiarum.Hoc rogant Charites, nouémque Musæ,Et Phœbus citharæ parens canoræ,Et quæ concutit Ægidem Minerua:Omnes illius hoc rogant amici.Olim non habuit sagacioresManus Cecropius faber, biformiQui monstro posuit vagas latebras,Errantésque vias domus nefandæ:Qui primas docuit volare ceras.Sphæræ non habuit senex repertorManus Archimedes peritiores, Qui Syracusias celebris arces Texit, atque diu nouis potentes Luísit artibus Italûm cateruas: Nostri Dedalea manus Duranti Quàm grato variant labore chartas, Quàm mutant varijs typos figuris. Prata sic variant suos colores: Flores sic variant suos odores. Ten' Chiragra feris nocere flagris Atque audire truces iuuat querelas? Inuisis lapidosa tunde nodis Pigros articulos, manúsque inertes. Desidum, licet, otiosa ventrum Cæde pondera tristibus flagellis, Qui sub Santonico cutem culullo Curant molliculam atque delicatam: Et quos Ganea, quos popina pernox Nudat lucifugos, tenebriones. Manus sanguineas preme, & nocentes, Auaras, rapidas, & impudicas Quæ tam spurca suis notant libellis, Tam turpes Veneres Cupidinésque. Istis si nequeas satis nocere, Pedes excruciet simul Podagra.
units.tr: Alas, Chiragra, fierce and raging evil, daughter of the Fury of Tartarus, who wearies mortals with dreadful, Stygian, savage and terrible torments, spare our Duranto, I beg you, I beg you. Spare him, and let it not be right that you harm the hands of one who is skilled in the hundred arts and the hundred refinements that they cultivate. The Graces ask this, and the nine Muses, and Phoebus, father of the tuneful lyre, and she who shakes the aegis, Minerva. All his friends ask this of you. Once the Cecropian craftsman, Daedalus, had no hands more skilful than these. He was the one who set up the wandering hiding place of the two-formed monster and the winding paths of the unspeakable house, and who first taught wax to fly. The old inventor of spheres, Archimedes, had no more skilful hands than these. He it was who fortified the famous citadel of Syracuse and long kept the Italian hordes in play with his new arts. Our Duranus's Daedalean hand, how pleasingly it varies the papers with its labour, how it changes the types with various figures! Thus meadows vary their colours, and flowers vary their scents. Does it please you, Chiragra, to harm these hands with savage whips and to listen to their fierce complaints? Strike with hateful knots the lazy, idle joints and the limp hands. Strike rather the idle bellies of the sluggards, with weighty blows and sorrowful lashes, of those who with Santonic wormwood cure their soft and delicate skin, and those whom the tavern and the all-night drinking-shop strip, the shunners of daylight, the shady fellows. Press hard upon the bloody, the harmful, the greedy, the rapacious and the shameless hands, which mark with such filthy books such shameful Venuses and Cupids. If you cannot harm these enough, let Podagra at the same time torment their feet.

units.la: MARTINI MARLOREI, BARRENSIS CAVSIDICI, Euangelicę veritatis persecutoris acerrimi,
units.tr: MARTIN MARLOREY, ADVOCATE OF BARR, THE MOST BITTER PERSECUTOR OF THE EVANGELICAL TRUTH,
EPITAPH.

units.la: ANdem Causidicum tacere Parca Iussit Marloreum bonis benigna, Quos Barri prius impotente lingua, Et gannitibus impijs, profanis, Impurus canis allatrauit vsque. Quos furens odio Vatiniano, Fictis criminibus, calumniisque, Longis vociferationibúsque Vexanit Sycophanta turbulentus, Inquietior Adria inquieto, Insanis violentior procellis, Thracio Diomede, vel Cyclope Humani sitientior cruoris, Poenis perfidior dolosiorque, Et Thrasone superbior Terentl, Iracundior inuido Catello, Interdum quoque blandior Catella, Vel risu meretricis exoletæ, Pica garrulior loquaciórve. Tandem Causidicus iacet, tacetque: Quem nihil cruciat magis peremptum, Quàm lingua modò quod simul perempta Posthac non poterit bonis nocere.
units.tr: The Parca, kind to good men, ordered this lawyer Marlorey to be silent at last. Before, at Barr, with an unrestrained tongue and impious, profane yelpings, the foul dog barked on at good men without ceasing. Raging with Vatinian hatred, the turbulent sycophant harassed them with fabricated charges and calumnies, with long clamours and outcries. He was more restless than the restless Adriatic, more violent than insane storms, more thirsty for human blood than Diomedes of Thrace or the Cyclops, more treacherous in punishments and more crafty in deceit, prouder than Thraso in Terence, more irascible than envious Catellus, and at times more fawning than a little bitch or the laughter of a worn-out whore, more chattering than a magpie and more loquacious. At last the lawyer lies dead and is silent: Nothing tortures him more, now that he is dead, than that his tongue, destroyed together with him, will no longer be able to harm good men.
TO JACOB LECTIUS.

units.la: LEctium Musa, Charitésque vestrum, Coniugis flentem modò funerata Fata crudeli properata casu Cernite vatem: Vtque lugentis lachrymas sodales Augeant fletu tepido madentes, Urbe cum tota, sileántque mœsti Funere tanto. Si lyra & nostris faciles fauetis Cantibus, tristi celerate amico Debitos versus: Helicone sacro Mittite carmen: Quod tuum tandem releuet dolorem, Quod tibi luctu querulo serenet Turbidos vultus, hilaréque frontem, Candide Lecti. Quæ ferox cunctos Libitina carpit: Quæ Duces æquat tenui superbos Pauperi, votis, precibúsque flecti Nescia puris, Coniugem dulci rapuit marito,
units.tr: Muses and Graces, look upon the poet who now weeps for his wife, whose fate was hastened by a cruel accident, so that the dead woman's companions may swell the tears of the mourner with warm weeping, and the whole city may fall silent in sorrow at so great a funeral. If the lyre, and you, the Muses, favour my songs, hasten the verses owed to your sad friend. Send a song from sacred Helicon that may at last relieve your grief, that may calm your troubled face and cheerful brow with mournful lament, Candidus Lectius. Savage Libitina, who levels the proud with the humble, has snatched away a wife from her sweet husband: a woman of chaste, gentle, modest character, made famous by outstanding piety, in the bloom of youth.

units.la: Moribus castis, placidis, pudicis:At que praestanti pietate claram,Flore iuuenta.
units.tr: She would have made you a father with beautiful children, and would have brought her ripening childbirths to light, if God, the fair arbiter of the great world, had wished it.

units.la: Illa te pulchra faceret parentemProle, maturos aperire partusSi Deus magni voluisset orbisArbiter aequus.
units.tr: But it seemed otherwise to the best of fathers, who had resolved that she should enter the seats above, and that the child hidden in its mother's womb should go with her.

units.la: Optimo visum est aliter Parenti,Qui simul sedes superas inireSanxerat matrem, & genitum latentemMatris in aluo.
units.tr: So, bestowing on the pious woman a better life, do you know with what joys he refreshes her, and how sweetly she is restored by the draught of nectar?

units.la: Sic piam vita potiore donansFoeminam, noftin' quibus aduocaritGaudiis, & quàm recreet suauiNectaris haustu?
units.tr: Now she enjoys the firm favour of the divinity; she fears no assaults of grief, nor does she shudder at the savage trumpets of raging Mars,

units.la: Illa nunc firmo fruitur fauoreNuminis: nullos metuit dolorumImpetus: nec dura furentis horretClassica Martis,
units.tr: who rages with violence through the whole world, who greedily lays waste the fields far and wide, who in his fury stains great cities with cruel slaughter.

units.la: Qui fremit toto violentum orbe,Qui rapax latè populatur agros,Qui feris magnas rabidus cruentatStragibus urbes.
units.tr: He who roars with violence through the whole world, who rapaciously ravages the fields far and wide, who rabid with wild slaughter stains great cities with bloodshed.

units.la: Illa nunc terras nitido iacentesDespicit caelo, vigilesque curasGentis humanae, & fugientis auiSomnia ridet.
units.tr: She now looks down from the bright sky upon the lands lying beneath her, and laughs at the restless cares of the human race and the dreams of fleeting life.

units.la: Vos inops auri cruciat cupido, Saeua vos tandem iugulat voluptas, Et sitis vani miseranda semper Torquet honoris: Laeta nunc dicit, meliúsque sponso Nupta caelesti veterem maritum Te vetat fletus, gemitum & querelas Fundere inanes.
units.tr: Greed for gold torments you, poor souls; cruel pleasure at last strangles you, and a pitiable thirst for empty honour forever racks you. The joyful bride now says, being wed to a better, heavenly bridegroom, and forbids you, who still have your old husband, to pour out tears, groans and vain complaints.

units.la: IN POLIÆNVM NVNC PRIMVM IN LVCEM EDITVM
units.tr: On Polyaenus, now first brought to light

units.la: Graecè ab Isaaco Casabonio Graecarum literarum in Academia Genevensi professore, Carmen Sapph.
units.tr: A Greek poem in Sapphic metre by Isaac Casaubon, professor of Greek literature in the Academy at Geneva.

units.la: Vnde nunc, Graecus superas reuisit Redditus luci Polyaenus auras? Vnde custodem Stygij fefellit Liminis atrum? Ecce pallentes Erebi tenebras Artium fugit veterum peritus, Quas duces olim docuit superbis Clarus in aulis. Vel redit tandem miserante Parca Perpetes doctae gemitus caterua. Et tuos, Graiis Casabone MusisGrate, labores.
units.tr: Whence has Polyaenus, the Greek, returned to the upper air and the light? Whence has he eluded the dark guardian of the Stygian threshold? Behold, the learned man, skilled in the ancient arts, has fled the pale shadows of Erebus, which once as a famous man in proud courts he taught to leaders. Or has the company of learned men, the ever-lasting groaning troop, returned at last, as Parca has pitied them? And your labours, Casaubon, dear to the Greek Muses.

units.la: Sic lyra dulcem modulante tristiNaeniam, iustisque Hecaten querelisMouit, & charam Eurydicen recepitThracius Orpheus.
units.tr: So the lyre, modulating a sad dirge with just laments, moved Hecate, and the Thracian Orpheus received back his beloved Eurydice.

units.la: Fallor, haud nigras Acheronlis anteMortuus vidit Polyanus umbras.Tertrium mitis vetat interireTurba sororum
units.tr: I am mistaken, unless Polyaenus, dead, has seen the dark shadows before Acheron. The gentle troop of sisters forbids the third to perish.

units.la: Laude quos virtus decorat perenni,Quos beant vires Genij benignae,Et quibus semper virides opacantTempora Lauri:
units.tr: Those whom virtue adorns with everlasting praise, whom the kindly powers of genius make blessed, and whose temples the green laurel always shades.

units.la: Sed diu caecis latitans cauernisPauit ignotus tineas inertes,Et situm tristem tulit indecoroPuluere tectus:
units.tr: But for a long time he lay hidden, unknown, in blind caverns, feeding on idle moths, and bore sad mould, covered with dust, in unseemly fashion.

units.la: Saeculi quum barbaries priorisArtibus bellis fera bella mouit,Et furens totum voluit per orbemPerdere Musas.
units.tr: When the barbarism of a former age waged fierce war on the arts, and, raging, wished to destroy the Muses throughout the whole world.

units.la: Ille tam saeui metuens pericli,Abditus claustris latitaret vsque,Et putri turpes carie puderetTollere vultus.
units.tr: He, fearing so cruel a danger, lay hidden behind closed doors, and was ashamed to raise his foul face, disfigured by rot.

units.la: Sed tuis tandem Casabone proditSumptibus liber, tetricosque linquens Carceres, docti nitet expolitus Pumicis arte. Nunc Ducum Graia memorare voce Bellicas laudes, simul & dolosi Abditos sensus reserare Martis Te Duce gestit. Perge sic clara veterum libellos, (Quos situs squallens premit, & tenebrae Nunc tegunt densa, retinentque vincla) Reddere luci, Sic tibi Musa faueant benignae, Sic placens te Phoebus amet, tuique Postera semper niteant labores Laude recentes.
units.tr: But at last, Casaubon, the book was brought forth at your expense, leaving behind its gloomy prisons, and shines, polished by the art of the learned pumice. Now it longs to recount in Greek speech the warlike praises of the leaders, and at the same time to unlock, under your guidance, the hidden meanings of deceitful Mars. Go on thus, illustrious one: restore to the light the books of the ancients, which squalid neglect presses down and darkness now covers with thick shadow and holds in chains. So may the kindly Muses favour you, so may Phoebus, pleased, love you, and may your later labours always shine, fresh with praise.

units.la: D. LECTIVM INVITAT VT NATO PVERO VELIT sponsor in baptismo esse.
units.tr: D. LECTIUS INVITES YOU, WHEN A BOY IS BORN, TO BE WILLING TO BE SPONSOR AT HIS BAPTISM.

units.la: Æc dies grato Superum fauore Me noua, Lecti, facit auctiorem Prole: quod notum tibi nuntiare Gestit amico.
units.tr: This day, by the favour of the gods above, makes me, Lectius, a new father, richer in offspring. I am eager to tell you this, my friend.
Poem: and if you see me, with an easy countenance, congratulating you,

units.la: Viderit vultu facili, rogareNe nouo certus renuas ParentiSponsor adesse:Quum recens sacris puer ablueturFontibus Christi: capietque ab illoNomen aeterna Monadis rigatusNomine trino.
units.tr: ask that you not refuse, but be certain to stand present as sponsor for the newborn, when the boy is recently to be washed in the sacred fountains of Christ and takes his name from him, bathed in the threefold name of the eternal Monad.

units.la: Nam suae Christus bonitatis olimSymbolum puris gregibus reliquitTale, quum sponsam proprio redeuntSanguine charam.
units.tr: For Christ long ago left such a token to his pure flocks, when he, returning with his own blood, reclaimed his beloved bride.

units.la: Atque primorum veteres parentumSustulit culpas meritamque mortem,Vt prius clausum reseraret altiLimen Olympi.
units.tr: He also removed the guilt of our first parents and their deserved death, so that he might unbar the high threshold of Olympus, which had been shut before.

units.la: Si volens, Lecti, tribuis quod opto,Quos amor Musae similis sodalesFecerat dudum potiora posthacFoedera iungent.
units.tr: If you willingly grant what I desire, Lectius, friends like those whom the love of the Muse once made similar to us will form even stronger bonds hereafter.

units.la: IOANNI ESYCHIO BRE- MENSI QVVM NOMEN MEVM in album amicorum reciperet.
units.tr: TO JOHANNES ESYCHIUS OF BREMEN, WHEN HE ADMITTED MY NAME INTO HIS ALBUM AMICORUM.

units.la: VNgamus ergo, ceu petis, Esychi Fidas amico foedere dexteras, Quod fraude iuratum remota Phoebus amet facilésque Musa.
units.tr: Let us then join hands, as you ask, Esychius, in a friendly covenant, a pledge sworn without deceit, which Phoebus and the gentle Muse both approve.

units.la: Unica vatum pectora nam probant Quos celsa Pindi culmina visere, Sacrosque fontes, & virentis Fronde volunt decorare lauri.
units.tr: For the hearts of the poets alike approve those whom the lofty peaks of Pindus invite to visit, and the sacred springs, and whom they wish to adorn with the green leaves of the laurel.

units.la: Sic, sic alumnos Pegasidum chori, Et quos eisdem sub penetralibus Eduxit aussex Phoebus, idem Nectat amor citharae placentis:
units.tr: Thus, thus, the foster-sons of the Pegasian choir, and those whom Phoebus, that same god, reared under the same shrine, love of the pleasing lyre binds together.

units.la: Sint ista nostri foederis Esychi Testes perennis carmina quae damus Túque, ô, fideli semper huius Sculpta sinu monumenta serua Ornate multis nominibus liber: Queis lucis addit perpetuae decus Doctrina Lipsi, quae per orbem Usque micat memorata totum.
units.tr: May these verses that we offer be witnesses of our covenant, Esychius, enduring, and may you, a book adorned with many names, keep these monuments engraved in your faithful bosom always; the teaching of Lipsius, which gleams throughout the whole world and is celebrated everywhere, adds glory to your light of lasting life.
JOHANNES ESYCHIUS OF BREMEN, TO JOHANNES IACOMOTUS.
Let us join our hearts, Iacomotus, let us join them and love one another.
Mutual love becomes the joined Muses, joined as they are.

units.la: Noster amor cultis, & amoenis coepit in hortis: Crescit florifero tempore consitus.
units.tr: Our love began in cultivated and pleasant gardens; it grows, planted in the flowering season.

units.la: Permulcétque meos sensus, & odoribus auras: His, his, tam nitidis vatibus inferor.
units.tr: It soothes my senses and perfumes the breezes with fragrance: I am second to these poets, so brilliant.

units.la: Atque placent docto Beza mea carmina, spirant Iacmoti lepidos iam quia spiritus.
units.tr: My verses please the learned Beza, and Iacomotus's charming spirit already breathes through them.

units.la: Iungamus Iacomote animos, iungamus, amemus: Quicquid Musa negat iunctus amor facit.
units.tr: Let us join our hearts, Iacomotus, let us join them and love one another: whatever the Muse refuses, joined love accomplishes.

units.la: CLAVDIO CVSSÆO LVRBINIO NOBILI GALLO, Geneuensium militum præfecto: ab expugnatione Clusæ in urbem reuertenti 21. Apr. 1590.
units.tr: To Claudius Cussæus Lurbinius, noble Frenchman, prefect of the Genevan soldiers, returning to the city from the capture of Clusa, 21 April 1590.

units.la: VOte decorum puluere Lurbini Recente cerno? Quæ noua nunc tuæ Laurus cohortu cingit umbra Conspicuas viridante frontes?
units.tr: Do I see Lurbinius back again, recently returned, dust-covered? What new laurel shade now wreathes your conspicuous brow with its green cohort?

units.la: Quo læta chari murmure nuntij Cunctis sonoros ædibus integrat Geneua plausus: perque templa Turba frequens Superum Parentem Non uisitatis laudibus euehit?
units.tr: Whereupon Geneva, glad at the cheerful murmur of the messengers, fills every house with resounding applause, and the crowd thronging the temples raises the Father of the gods with praises not usually heard?

units.la: Arces reuulsas te duce rupibus Audit tremendis, & patere Claustra tuo superata marte.
units.tr: She hears that the citadels were torn from their rocks under your leadership, and that the barriers, overcome by your martial valour, lie open.

units.la: Quæ fastuoso Regulus Allobrox Fidens Iberum fœdere struxerat, Tetrisque Iurassi rigentis Abdita munierat cauernis, Non caciores incoluit specus
units.tr: The stronghold which the proud Allobrogian chieftain had built, trusting in the Spaniard's alliance, and had fortified with the grim hidden caverns of the frozen Jura, was not inhabited by a more loathsome den.
The monstrous beast Cacus, the Iberian,
when he deceived the returning son of Amphitryon
with his treacherous arts,
stealing the herds and
hiding them in the sulphurous hollows of Aniro,
the thief from whose mouth he belched blazing flames,
vigilant with his terrifying face.

units.la: Non ille furtum, non tulit hoc scelus
units.tr: He did not carry off this theft and crime
with impunity, for he felt
what the well-known valour and what the club
of Hercules, dreaded by wild monsters, could do.
When the treacherous violence of the Savoyard soldier
held the caves on equal terms,

units.la: Heu! quanta late tunc per agros
units.tr: alas, how great the damage he dealt to our people
as he rushed far and wide across the fields!
When the Allobrogian prince, stronger with his overwhelming host,
burst forth with such spirit,
and the Spanish phalanxes,
and the purple band of the Italians.
Ocean's swelling waves bring no greater evils
when they break through the barriers,
nor the Rhine's stagnant water
when, poured out, it carries off the Batavian harvests.
Winds do not rush more grimly across the sea

units.la: Venti per aequor, quum ciet Aeolus
units.tr: when Aeolus stirs up
great storms, and shakes the hearts
of sailors with restless fear.
He drove off the booty and plundered the houses,

units.la: Raptásque stupris polluit insolens Hostis maritas, virginésque: Non scelere abstinuit nefando.
units.tr: and the insolent enemy, polluting married women and virgins by seizing them in debauchery, did not refrain from unspeakable crime.

units.la: Quod magna summi dextera vindicis Frata prisco tempore punijt Quum vertit infames Sodomas Æthereum iaculata sulphur.
units.tr: What the great right hand of the supreme avenger punished in former times, when he overturned infamous Sodom, hurling ethereal sulphur.

units.la: Quas pleniori copia fuderat Per arua cornu largáque faustitas Fruges & vndantis Lyæi Dona ferox sibi vindicauit.
units.tr: The crops and abundant prosperity which he had poured over the fields in fuller plenty from the horn, and the gifts of the surging Lyaeus, the fierce man claimed for himself.

units.la: Boum labores perdidit & sata Flammisque pagos subiciens vagis Incendit & semen paratum Credere humo vetuit feraci.
units.tr: He destroyed the labours of the oxen and the crops, setting the villages on fire with wandering flames, and forbade the seed prepared for the fertile earth to be entrusted to the soil.

units.la: Quæ dixit atrox, Versoui simul Vallauit arces: tuta nec amplius Nauis per obsessi Lemanni Cærule as volitauit vndas!
units.tr: These were the savage words: "We have turned about and surrounded the citadels"; and no longer does the safe ship fly over the blue waves of besieged Lake Geneva!

units.la: Geneua vitias esurie manus Nunc tendet exspes: libera nunc iugo Subdet Sabaudo colla, nostris Seruiet imperiys subasta.
units.tr: Geneva, now starving, will stretch out her hands in empty hope; now free, she will bend her neck to the Savoyard yoke and, put up for sale, will serve our commands.

units.la: Cœli sed alto vertice qui sedet Orbémque iustis arbitriis regit Iras Tyranni tam cruentas Spésq; trucésque minas repressit.
units.tr: But he who sits on the high summit of heaven and rules the world by just decrees has checked the tyrant's wrath, so bloody, and his grim threats and hopes.
When, in narrow straits, Geneva showed you a breast undaunted,

units.la: Geneua peſlus præbuit,& feriTraſtare Gradiui potentemLurbinium truculenta bella.
units.tr: Geneva offered a fearless breast, and you, Lurbinius, powerful in the cruel wars of Gradivus (Mars), waged fierce wars.

units.la: Cui quum regendas auſpiciis daresTuis cohortes exiguas,furensPer omne tunc miles periclumVsque ruit meliore duſtu.
units.tr: To whom, when under your auspices you gave small cohorts to command, the soldier rushed through every danger everywhere with better leadership.

units.la: Quæ iam tuorum pro patria moriVirtus armabat ſtrenua ciuiumTunc ſæpius viſtis SabaudumClarior emicuit cateruis.
units.tr: The valour of your citizens, eager to die for their country, then armed and more often seen, shone more brightly among the Savoyard troops.

units.la: O quàm ſuperbo Uerſouium impetuIrrupit audax! Hic cecidit feroxHiſpana per vicos iuuentusHic Italum periere turmæ.
units.tr: O with what bold impetus you burst upon proud Versoix! Here the fierce Spanish youth fell through the streets; here the Italian troops perished.

units.la: Triſtem Lemannus tunc poſuit metum,Ruptíque vinclis tunc ſua nauibusSulcanda reddens terga tutumStrauit iter vitreum per æquor.
units.tr: Lake Geneva then laid aside its dread, and its ships, released from their chains, offered their furrowed backs and laid a safe glassy path across the sea.

units.la: Lætuſque noſtris portubus intulitQuæ ſubiugato cœperat oppidoTormenta viſtrix ſena pubes,Allobrogum exuuias opimas.
units.tr: And the victorious band of six companies, glad, brought into our harbours the rich spoils of the Allobroges, and the artillery which had begun in the subjugated town.

units.la: Vicina queis mox Baſtia corruitQuaſſata,& arcis mœnia Gayi:Turriſque diros quæ latronesExcita monticulo f uebatIſtis reclusa nunc quoque machinis
units.tr: By these engines, too, Bastie soon collapsed, shattered, and the walls of the castle of Gaix; and the towers which the dire robbers held from their little hill were opened.

units.la: Tristes latebræ, claustraque montibus Obtecta, non nostræ minaces Insidias meditantur urbi. Sic tu Geneuam Cœlituum Pater Præsente semper Numine sospita Cunctisque seruatum periclis Protege Lurbinium precamur. Ducis superbi perge ferociam, Fastusque forti tundere brachio Ut urbe tuta te decoris Incolumes celebremus hymnis.
units.tr: The grim hiding-places and passes hidden by the mountains no longer plot menacing ambushes against our city. Thus, Father of the heavenly ones, ever present in power, we pray you keep Geneva safe and protect Lurbinius, preserved from all dangers. Continue to crush the proud leader's ferocity and pride with your strong arm, so that, with the city safe, we may celebrate you, unharmed, with hymns of praise.

units.la: NICOLAO HARLÆO INTERIORIS CONSILII REGII Consiliario: Turmæ equitum præfecto: & militiæ Regię aduersus Sabaudię Ducem Legato.
units.tr: To Nicolaus Harlaeus, Councillor of the Inner Royal Council, Prefect of a Troop of Horse, and Royal Envoy in the Army against the Duke of Savoy.

units.la: HArlaæ duro tempore cui fides, Virtusque Francis cognita regibus Illustre per seras nepotum Progenies feret vsque nomen.
units.tr: Harlaeus, to whom faith and courage, known to the kings of France, come in these harsh times, the illustrious progeny of later generations will carry your name through the distant ages.

units.la: Me Musa cogit tendere barbiton Iani Calendis: queis remeans noua Phœbus renascentem fouere Purpureus face gestit annum.
units.tr: The Muse compels me to tune my lyre on the Calends of January, when Phoebus, returning, glows purple and eager to warm the newly born year with his torch.

units.la: Et læta festas Æolio iubet Tibi salutes dicere pectine: Te cura pro charis Geneua Solicitum licet inquieta Muris fatiget: dum procul improbos Nostris Sabaudi pellere finibus Tentas furores: & morantes Hic nimium remouere belli Causas furentis. Nil strepitus lyra
units.tr: And, joyful, she bids me offer you festive greetings on the Aeolian lyre. Though Geneva, anxious on your behalf, wearies you with restless care on her walls, you, far off, strive to drive the wicked rage of Savoy from our borders, and to remove the causes of a raging war that have delayed too long. The noise of the lyre

units.la: Dulceis sonora magnanimis Ducum Coeptis nocebunt: nec frementes Docta tubas animare Musa. Quum corda vellit grandia fortium. Quum mentis alta promouet impetus: Et laude clarorum perenni Facta virûm decoranda saeclis Tollit futuris. Non Phariae suos Ornant Tyrannos pyramides magis. Non sculpta Mausolea sumptu Magnifico monimenta Carum Regem celebrant. Non magis aethere Pendentium alto magna Semiramin Commendat hortorum, aut sepulchri Structa viro Babylone moles. Charas Auorum tristis imagines Delet vetustas, aeraque fortior Antiqua, caelatosque vultus Dente terit Caries superbo: Imbresve nymbis qui gelidi ruunt: Aut quos Rubentis robore brachij Commotus ignes Rex suprema Caelituum iaculatur arce. Attrita tandem marmora concidunt, Arcusque celsis nubibus aemuli. Hac cuncta Saturnus resecta Falce truci violentus aufert. Quos funeranit liuida mors statim
units.tr: will not harm the sweet-sounding enterprises of great-hearted commanders, nor will the Muse, skilled in song, rouse the trumpets that roar. When it stirs the great hearts of brave men, when it raises the high impulses of the mind, and with the everlasting praise of famous men it lifts up deeds of men to be adorned for future ages. The Pharian pyramids do not adorn their tyrants more. Carved mausoleums built at great cost do not commemorate a dear king more. Nor does the lofty hanging garden of Semiramis, nor the mass of Babylon built for a man, commend him more to the sky. Old age destroys the dear images of ancestors, and ancient bronze, though stronger, and carved faces are ground down by the proud tooth of decay, as are the showers of icy rain that fall with the storm, or the fires which the king of the gods hurls from his lofty citadel, kindled by the strength of his blazing arm. At last the worn marbles collapse, and arches that rival the lofty clouds. Savage Saturn, with his cruel scythe, carries off all these things by force. Livid death immediately tries to drown those whom it has laid low in the forgetful river, and to bury them in the perpetual night of Avernus, mixed with its waters.

units.la: Obliuioso flumine mergereConatur, immistisque AuerniPerpetua sepelire nocte.
Sed laude dignum, & quem meritis sonantClarum Camœnæ: Pieridum & fauorExtollit almus, ridet illeIura stygis truculenta furuæ:
units.tr: But the one worthy of praise, whom the Muses make famous with deserved renown, whom the kindly favour of the Pierides exalts, laughs at the savage laws of the grim Fury of the Styx.

units.la: Sæuósque morsus temporis inuidi,Mortésque vitat, carminis aliteSi fama subuectum sonoroPer memores canat vsque fastos.
units.tr: And he avoids the cruel bites of envious time and death, if the fame of the song-bird, borne aloft on sonorous verse, sings him through the mindful annals for ever.

units.la: Quid? sola cunctis Calliope potestMonstrare terris te celebrem: tuaSi facta venturo disertisCarminibus memorârit ævo.
units.tr: What then? Calliope alone has the power to make you known to the lands, if she has recorded your deeds in eloquent songs for the age to come.

units.la: Vt (fastuosis quum LotharingicæTe Gentis olim seditionibusRex iussit expertus fidelemHelueticas properare ad vrbes)
units.tr: As (when the Lorraine people, in their proud seditions, once tested you, the king ordered you, as a trusted man, to hasten to the Swiss cities)

units.la: Velox Geneuam tramite deuioPromptam aduolasti iungere dexteras,Regique prouisum paratamAuxilium dare fœderato.
units.tr: you swiftly flew by a winding path to Geneva, ready to join right hands, and to give the king, our ally, the help he had foreseen and prepared.

units.la: Atque hinc feraces Helueticæ petensAgros propinquæ, Marte ferociaMox corda Gentis compulistiTendere opem sociásque vires.
units.tr: And from there, seeking the fertile fields of the neighbouring Swiss, you soon, with fierce warfare, drove that people's hearts to extend aid and allied forces.
Thus surrounded by a band of keen young men:
And the French standards following the Rhaetians
suddenly through the borders of Savoy
you wage war, feared by the enemy.
And breaking the high ramparts of the Riparia
chains unknown to our walls
threatening ships and Lake Geneva
servitude, with crackling flame,
you destroy; and, foreseeing, you check the hopes of the enemy
and, as victor, beat back their vain assault,
and force the harassed Allobroges
to tremble in bloody war.
And you would at once have brought many more advantages
to the city; but the king, fearing for himself,
wished to hasten
all the troops of the allied people.
Now Geneva, happier after your various adventures, sees you returned,
and, at your peril, feels that you have redeemed
the peace, and, anxious, are recalling it.
Those things which the violence of the Duke of Savoy
long ago tore away, while he eagerly
seeks to enlarge his own borders, and burning
plans to press our necks beneath his yoke
with grim intent, while he delights in impious
rebellions and nefarious
disturbances through the fields of the troubled Gauls,
he fiercely rejoices in renewing the uprisings.
Where are you bound, bold lyre? Cease at last to delay the public business.

units.la: T andem morari tempora barbite:Longo nec Harlaum gerentemBella velis retinere uersu.Forsan superbas fortior hoftiumPellit phalanges. Nunc fatis illiusOptare prouisis benignosConfilijs Superum fauores.
units.tr: Lyre, at last cease to delay the times; nor with a long verse wish to hold back Harlaeus, who bears the wars. Perhaps, braver, he will drive back the proud phalanxes of the enemy. Now, with the fates provided for him, pray for the kindly favour of the gods upon his counsels.

units.la: GRATVLATORIVM CARMEN AD CLARISSIMVM VIrum D. Ioannem Anthonium Sarracenum artis Medicae peritissimum: quum Lucretiam Blandratam honestissimis parentibus natam in vxorem duxisset 6. Cal. feb. Ann. CIO. IO. XCI.
units.tr: CONGRATULATORY POEM TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN, Mr. Johann Anthony Sarracenus, most skilled in the medical art, when he had taken Lucretia Blandrata, born of most honourable parents, as his wife, on 6 Cal. Feb., in the year 1591.

units.la: ESTA quid resonem dieQuae te coniugio reddituni amabili.Gestit cernere blandiorSarracene caput Pegasidum chorisDilectum, & medicae decusArtis conspicuum quam PodaleiriusHumanum docuit genus
units.tr: Why should I sing of this day, which returns you to a lovely marriage? Sarracenus, head of the Pegasian choirs, beloved and conspicuous glory of the medical art, which Podaleirius taught to the human race, rejoices to see you.
What vow shall I make for you in my songs?
Or what will Hymen sing upon the lyre?
O you who, creator of all things, gave the everlasting laws of wedlock
and first sanctioned the covenants and sweet bonds of a mutual bed,
May the auspicer keep you safe with your new wife
under a fortunate omen.
And may his favour will you to be happy
in the unbroken bond,
may chaste matronly modesty join your hearts
with the bright loves of you both.
May quarrels and grievous complaints
not part your harmonious minds.
Not that tongue of an envious race, born in the Tartarean marshes,
which with cruel suspicions vexes tender minds;
may no stronger yoke of bronze ever part you.
What can the human race pluck more sweetly than the nuptial beds
which unbroken faith cherishes,
which piety and fear of the gods consecrate?
When the husband cherishes his one bride,
and the wife, fearing another man, looks up to her one husband
and hears no gleaming adulterers,
but nurses offspring like the father,
happier at the milky breast;
and delights in the home,
and wisely manages whatever labour the husband brings in
and disposes of it well.
But let the race hateful to God perish wretchedly,
the bold race that forbids marriage,
which, pretending with vain religions,
impiously condemns the worship of the heavenly ones,
and the lawful torches of marriage.
It thinks that by a celibate life
it is planted in the seats of the gods by its merits.
Does not the foul stream of crimes, bursting forth from these filthy springs,
usually defile the homes?
Does not this virginity, once vowed, pollute the streets of cities with its debaucheries,
and stain the cloisters with horrid murders?
But the people that has learned to obey pure laws
drives far off the dogmas of the demon
and the painted deceits
of the Stygian (fury); nor does it count it a sin,
conscious of the Olympian light,
to enjoy the gifts granted by the heavenly ones.
TO THE SAME MAN.

units.la: ORnatura diu non mittunt Pharmacopola Sarracene tuum munera connubium. Nam dicto citius rapidis gula dentibus illa Luxus & immitis cuncta vorare solet. Sed forsan qua dona tibi nunc parvula mitto Sunt mansura olim, sunt placitura simul. Exornent mensas bellaria lauta secundas, Illustrat sacras clara Camoena faces.
units.tr: Saracen apothecaries do not for long send their adorning gifts for your wedding, for greed and fierce luxury, quicker than a word, devours everything with its rapid teeth. But perhaps the small gifts I now send you will endure in time and please at once. Let delicious sweetmeats adorn your second courses; the bright Muse lights the sacred torches.

units.la: IOANNI IONSTONO SCOTO AD SACRVM VERBI Dei ministerium exercendum in patriam reuertenti 9. Mart. 1591.
units.tr: TO JOHN JONSTON OF SCOTLAND, ON HIS RETURN TO HIS COUNTRY TO EXERCISE THE SACRED MINISTRY OF THE WORD, 9 March 1591.

units.la: ERgo Caledonia fines Ionstone reuisis, Et dulcis arua patriæ? Ergo paras tandem cœlesti nectare sacrum Ovile Christi pascere: Cœtibus atque piis fœcundo pectore iura Legis supremæ promere?
units.tr: Is it then, Jonston, that you revisit the borders of Caledonia and the sweet fields of your homeland? Is it then that you at last prepare to feed Christ's sacred fold with heavenly nectar, and with a fruitful heart to set forth to pious assemblies the laws of the supreme Law?
Well done!

units.la: Macte animi Ionstone via hac te ducet ad astra,Diuumque mensis asseret.
units.tr: Well done, Jonston, brave of spirit! This way will lead you to the stars and will install you at the tables of the gods.

units.la: Ne longum te turbet iter, nec tempora bellisVbique dura tristibus.
units.tr: Let not the long journey trouble you, nor the times, harsh with wars and sad everywhere.

units.la: Ille erit, ille comes qui te vocat, i pede faustoQuocunque te Deus iubet.
units.tr: He will be the companion, he who calls you. Go with a lucky foot wherever God bids you.

units.la: Hoc duce Sauromatas tutus, pictosq; Agathyrsos,Propontidisque Bosphorum:
units.tr: With him as your leader you will be safe among the Sauromatians and the painted Agathyrsi, and at the Bosphorus of the Propontis.

units.la: Indosque assiduis innise caloribus vstosInhospitalem & Caucasum.
units.tr: You will also tread among the Indians, scorched by ceaseless heat, and the inhospitable Caucasus.

units.la: Nec metue Oceani fluctus, ventosque furentes:Et monstra Ponto quæ natant.
units.tr: Do not fear the waves of the Ocean or the raging winds, nor the monsters that swim in the Pontus.

units.la: Auspicio quem Christe tuo comitaris euntemNon oscines coruos timet,
units.tr: The one you accompany, O Christ, as he goes under your auspices, does not fear the ill-omened ravens.

units.la: Prægnantisq; canis, Parrhæ aut recinentis iniquūNon horret omen obuium.
units.tr: Nor does he shudder at the pregnant bitch, or at the unlucky omen of the Parrhasian bird that answers back, or at any omen that meets him.

units.la: Quid? ridet portenta simul quæ Thuscus AruspexVanique monstrant Augures.
units.tr: What then? He laughs at the portents which the Tuscan haruspex points out, and the vain augurs too.
G

units.la: PAVLO MELISSO POETÆ CELEBERRIMO, QVVM PER literas à D. Beza petiisset sibi nomen indicari, quod notabatur tribus literis I. I. B. in quibusdam versibus anno 1590. emissis.
units.tr: To Paulus Melissus, the most celebrated poet, when at Beza's request by letter he had asked to be told the name which was indicated by the three letters I. I. B. in certain verses published in the year 1590.

units.la: {M}Vsis orte bonis, Melisse, vatum Quos Germania fert decus perenne: Cui cingunt meritum caput Corollæ Lauri Cæsarea manu plicatæ, Cur nostrum tibi poscis explicari Nomen, quod notulis tribus minutis Signatum sibi vindicat pudenter Paucos versiculos, inelegantes Rudes, illepidos, & impolitos Expertes venerum, & suauitatum Quales vsque tuis nitent libellis, Doctis & lepidis, & expolitis?
units.tr: You, Melissus, born for the good fortune of poets, whom Germany bears as an everlasting glory, whose deserving head is encircled by a garland of laurel woven by the Caesarean hand: why do you demand that there be explained to you our name, which, marked by three small letters, modestly claims for itself a few little verses, crude, unpolished, unrefined, lacking charm and grace, such as always shine in your books, learned and elegant and polished?

units.la: Ne iustam tibi mouerint timemus Nauseam & reliquis bonis poetis Gerrarum leuium soni canori Gerris Trinacriis ineptiores, Versus pondere qui carent & arte, Quales temporibus Maronis olim Manios Mæuius Baniúsque scriptitabant.
units.tr: Lest we should fear that the just disgust of you and of the other good poets might be aroused by the sounds of light Gerrae, more inept than the Sicilian gerrae, verses lacking weight and art, such as Mævius and Bavius once used to scribble in the times of Maro.

units.la: Sed qui Beza tuis fauet Camœnis,Qui te semper amat, bonosque vates,Cui nihil insipidum sapiunt vnquam,Qui quod illepidum est, & inuenustumNon dicit lepidum esse vel venustum,Qui nostras aliquid putant esseNugas, me vetuit timere quicquam.Nam pectus tibi moribus vetustisEt candore animi benigniorisEsse non minus asserit politumQuàm rara simul eruditione.Quid? nugas tibi displicere posseNegat quas probat & legit libenter.
units.tr: But Beza, who favours your Muses, who always loves you and the good poets, to whom nothing ever tastes insipid, who does not call what is unrefined and unlovely refined or lovely, who think our trifles are something, has forbidden me to fear anything at all. For he asserts that your breast, through its ancient manners and the candour of a kinder mind, is no less polished than it is rare in learning. What? He denies that trifles could displease you, when you approve of them and read them gladly.

units.la: AD THEOPHILVM QVATIGRANVM TEMPENSEM AMICISSIMVM, & Ecclesiasten diligentissimum.
units.tr: TO THEOPHILUS QUATIGRANUS OF TEMPE, MY MOST DEAR FRIEND, AND A MOST DILIGENT ECCLESIASTES.

units.la: VIste nunc grauioribusDefessum studiis vmbrifero in specu,Musarum recreat chorus?Quis te lauricomos nunc QuatigranieDucit Phœbus in Aonas?Deceptum citharæ dulcis amoribus?
units.tr: Does the chorus of the Muses now refresh you, wearied with weightier studies, in the shady cave? Or does Phoebus now lead you, Quatigranus, laurel-crowned, into the Aonian haunts, deceived by the sweet loves of the lyre?

units.la: Quod te nunc opus occupat? Quod tractas vigili mente negotium? Nam te mollis inertia Non unquam potuit fallere, nec leuis Somni languidior mora. Sed te nobilior cura laboribus Exercere bonis solet: Seu qua magniloquus non facili via Olim dißerunt scholis Stagirita suis quaerere te iuuat, Atque ingens Anyti reus: Qui risum simulans Cecropia improbos Gentis carpsit acerbius Mores, qui vitium tollere dum studet Occultum, inuidia obrutus Tandem lethiferis morsibus occidit. Seu tu Mincigena potens Vates grandisonam Vergilij tubam Inflas, qua cecinit pium Æneam Ausonij carminis alite, Incenso quod ab Ilio Hostes per medios telaque plurima Grandaeuum eripuit patrem. Seu docto gracilem pollice barbiton Flacci concutis aemulus, Lauro digna sonans carmina perpete. Vrget strenua sed magis Pectus cura tuum, teque per arduos Pellit
units.tr: What work now occupies you? What business do you handle with a watchful mind? For soft idleness has never been able to deceive you, nor the more languid delay of sleep. But a nobler care is wont to exercise you with good labours: whether it pleases you to seek, by the hard way the great-speaking Stagirite once set out in his schools; or the mighty accused Anytus, who, feigning laughter, too bitterly bit the wicked manners of the Cecropian people, and who, while he strove to remove a hidden vice, overwhelmed by envy, at last died by deadly bites; or whether you, a powerful poet born on the Mincius, blow the grandly sounding trumpet of Vergil, with which he sang of pious Aeneas, the bird of Ausonian song, who rescued his aged father from burning Troy through the midst of enemies and many missiles; or whether, emulating Flaccus, you strike the slender lyre with a learned thumb, sounding songs worthy of perpetual laurel. But a vigorous care presses your heart more strongly, and drives you

units.la: Pellit quaerere tramitesLucis sydereas splendidius iubar:Dum prudens aurea manuVersas scripta sacris dogmata vatibusUt Pastor gregibus suaFidus Christicolis pabula porrigas.Hic nostras QuatigraneMentes perpetuus sollicitet labor:Qui verum decus afferat,Aeternaque piis laetitia bonum.Quid rerum tenues inuatUmbras, & fluida somnia persequiVita, aut ludicra, quae rapitEffrenis subiti temporis impetus?
units.tr: drives you to seek, by steep paths, the brighter light of the starry sun, while with a prudent hand you turn the sacred writings of the prophets into golden doctrines, as a faithful pastor offers food to his flock of Christians. May this unceasing labour trouble our Quatigranus' mind: a labour that brings true glory and eternal joy, a good to the pious. Why do you care to pursue the slight shadows of things and fleeting dreams, or a life of play, which the unbridled rush of sudden time carries away?
TO JOHN POLYANDRIUS, RETURNING TO HIS COUNTRY

units.la: ut munus Ecclesiasticum obiret 16. die Mensis Febr. 1591.
units.tr: that he might take up the ecclesiastical office, on 16 February 1591.

units.la: VVM te patria nunc vocetTellus: atque gregi te cupiat pioSacri pabula nectaris,Succosque Ambrosiae promere perpetes,Ifausto pede. Quo Deus
units.tr: Since your native land now calls you, and desires you to offer her flock the holy food of nectar and to draw out the everlasting juices of Ambrosia, go with a fortunate foot, where God

units.la: Certum monstrat iter, tende lubens, simulSegnes tolle moras. Duce
units.tr: shows the sure road. Go gladly, and at the same time cast off sluggish delays. Lead

units.la: Quid caelo metuis? Quid PolyandriumPatrem Iane times sequi,
units.tr: Why do you fear heaven? Why, John, do you fear to follow the father Polyandrius,

units.la: Quem clarat pietas, quem celebrat fidesChristi nutibus obsequens?
units.tr: whom piety makes famous, and whom faith, obedient to the nods of Christ, celebrates?

units.la: O, nunc turpe scelus pellere destina,Et furua tenebras stygis,
units.tr: O, now resolve to drive away the shameful crime, and the dark shadows of the Styx,

units.la: Passim Romulidum quas violentiaSparsit Pontificum impotens,
units.tr: which the violence of the Papists, impotent pontiffs, has scattered everywhere,

units.la: Et lucis supera non patiens furor.Ne quid splendidius putes
units.tr: and the furious rage that does not suffer the light above. Do not think anything more splendid

units.la: Quam seruire Deo, Caelituum & patiPromptis pectoribus iugum:
units.tr: than to serve God, and with ready hearts to bear the yoke of the heavenly ones,

units.la: Atque illos meritis tollere honoribus.Foelices ter & amplius
units.tr: and to raise them to honours by merit. Thrice happy and more

units.la: Puram syderea queis face veritasMentem lustrat, ut inclytis
units.tr: are those whose truth, with a starry torch, purifies the mind, so that by famous labours
they may be able to subdue the fierce monsters of errors,

units.la: Et nubem dubiis demere mentibusQuae solis iubar aureum
units.tr: and to remove from doubting minds the cloud which obscures the golden light of the sun

units.la: Fusc t perpetui, sacraque lumina:Nec cerni patitur viam,
units.tr: and the sacred lights of the everlasting one, and does not allow the way to be seen

units.la: Quae certo Superum lactea tramiteSedes ducit ad arduas.
units.tr: which leads by the certain milky path of the Most High to the lofty abodes,

units.la: Et summa referat praemia gloriae.Laudatur vagus Hercules,
units.tr: and brings back the highest rewards of glory. Wandering Hercules is praised
because with the fierce strength of his club
he crushed many monsters of old,
and with iron and bright fires destroyed
the Lernaean serpents, a wild pest,
infamous; and having tamed the robbers
and monstrous tyranny,
he restored the pressed cities to fruitful peace
and the strong and harmful
imposing bridles on licence, which is too powerful.
Theseus is praised
by ever-fresh fame, the house of Daedalus,
because he boldly penetrated
the dark approaches and blind thresholds;
and the infamous adulteress's
offspring, Pasiphae's, he pressed upon the Athenians,
destroying the imposed yoke,
and the sad commands of the Cretan leader.
But a nobler praise remains
on the lofty heights of the star-bearing pole,
for those who strongly overcome vice,
who cut away the wiles of Tartarean Dis
and the lies, by which fitting
glory is rendered to the divine Power above.

units.la: ABRAHAMO HENRICO NORMANO Θαμύδιον IANUARIJ mensis die 15. An. 1591.
units.tr: To Abraham Henry Norman, Thamudion [Θαμύδιον], 15 January 1591.

units.la: QVÆ te flere iubet patrem Extinctum pietas: hæc eadem modum Iustis ponere luctibus Præscribit, rigidis atque doloribus Indulgere bonos vetat.
units.tr: The piety that bids you weep for your dead father also prescribes a measure for just mourning, and forbids good men to indulge in harsh and painful grief.

units.la: Henrice, & lachrymas fundere perpetes. Quorum pectoribus nitet Puris syderea lux Sapientiæ: Et quos Cœlituum sacris Prompta mente iuvat legibus obsequi, Fletu si tumulos rigant, Si tundunt modicis pectora planctibus Illos certa fides fovet, Solatúrque dies ultima quæ bonos Tandem moribus eximens, Exspectata piis præmia cœtibus Æternúmque feret decus.
units.tr: Henry, and to pour out tears without end? For those in whose pure breasts shines the starry light of wisdom, and who gladly obey with ready mind the sacred laws of the heavenly ones: if they water the tombs with weeping, if they beat their breasts with moderate laments, a sure faith cherishes them. The last day, which at length takes good men out of their mortal lives, consoles them, and brings the reward awaited by the pious assembly, and an eternal glory.

units.la: Sed Gentes superi Numinis insciæ Quæ fictos metuunt deos, Impuríque simul Tartareum colunt Vanæ Dæmona ritibus: Et quorum ambiguas error imagine Mentes ludificat vaga Nil vita melius, morte nihil putant Pœnas, quæ nigricantibus Vmbris cuncta domat, gaudia quæ brevis Ævi falsa metit ferox. Hinc longis repetunt questibus, horrido Quem mors frigore percutit. Huic conducta sonat Præfica nænias Tristes: hinc vlulatibus Funestas quatiunt terrificis nurus Ædes, & miseris thoros Lugentes viduos fletibus obruunt, Sævisque unguibus efferæ Discerpuntque comas, & lacerant genas. Nam quæ summa benignitas Largitur Superùm Christicolis: simul Qua cælum petitur via Gens ignara Dei, cæcáque non videt. Nostris sed stygias Pater Cœlestis tenebras mentibus abstulit Monstrauitque simul sacræ Quæ Gentis sequitur gloria liuidas Mortes, quantâque faustitas. Sic post dura tibi funera nunc parens Arces attigit igneas: Fœlixque æthereo nectare vescitur: Et quas quaesier at polo Nunc miratur opes flammigero micans Semper, nec gemitus probat Nunc Henrice tuos, nec querimonias.
units.tr: But the nations ignorant of the supreme God, who fear feigned gods and impiously worship together the Tartarean demon with vain rites, and whose minds the wandering error of deceptive images mocks, think nothing better than life and nothing of punishment after death, which the dark shadows subdue, and which the fierce one reaps as the false joys of a brief life. Hence they repeat their long laments over him whom death strikes with horrid cold. For him a hired mourner sounds dismal dirges; hence the daughters-in-law shake the house with terrifying howls, and the grieving widows overwhelm the wretched marriage bed with tears, and the savage women tear their hair with cruel nails and lacerate their cheeks. For the supreme kindness of the gods bestows on Christians what the nation ignorant of God does not see, and what is hidden from it: the way by which heaven is sought. But our heavenly Father has removed the Stygian darkness from our minds, and has shown at the same time the glory that follows the sacred nation, and how death's livid face is outweighed by its great happiness. So now, after your harsh funeral, your father has reached the fiery citadels, and happily feasts on heavenly nectar, and now marvels at the riches he sought in the sky, shining ever with flame; and he does not approve, Henry, of your groans or your complaints.

units.la: AD DANIELEM ROSETVM GENEVENSEM, VXORIS meae nepotem, de ficu mortua 1591.
units.tr: TO DANIEL ROSETUS OF GENEVA, GRANDSON OF MY WIFE, ON THE DEAD FIG TREE, 1591.

units.la: MITTO fata tibi, Rosete, ficus Deplorata meae dolente plectro. Quid? frontem caperas? Seueriores Interdum licet abdicare musas, Et cantare iocos, facetiásque Iucundus, lepidas, simúlque honestas. Quae nunquam noceant sed vsque prosint. Versu Maeonides disertiore Ranarum retulit cruenta bella. Quid? Maro Latiae decus Camoenae, Qui Troiae cecinit graues ruinas, Æneamq; pium diu per vndas Iactatum æquoreas truci procella: Descripsit varij dapes moreti,
units.tr: I send you, Rosetus, the fate of my fig tree, mourned on my grieving lyre. What? Are you frowning? Sometimes it is permitted to set aside the sterner Muses and sing playful things, witty and pleasant trifles, which never harm but always benefit. The Maeonian, in a more eloquent verse, recounted the bloody wars of the frogs. What? Maro, the glory of the Latin Muse, who sang of the grievous ruins of Troy and of pious Aeneas, long tossed over the waves by a fierce storm, described the humble dishes of the peasant Moretus.

units.la: Et paruum culicem, leuésque nugas. Luxit carmine passerem Catullus Extinctum querulo sua puella. Sic suetam liceat dolere ficum Nobis nectareas referre ficos, Atque umbras dare frondibus venustis (Dum vixit) virides, vigente sole Quid? si commoda pensitare mecum Mente cuncta voles serenior, Quae ficus mea proferebat olim, Hic me ludere fortiter negabis: Nec fictas lachrymas meas putabis.
units.tr: And the little gnat and light trifles. Catullus lamented in verse the sparrow of his girl, dead and mourned with a plaintive song. So may it be permitted to me to grieve for the fig tree, which used to bear nectar-sweet figs for us and gave green shade with its lovely leaves (while it lived) under the flourishing sun. What? If you will weigh all its benefits with me in a calmer mind, you will deny that I am playing boldly here, and you will not think my tears feigned.

units.la: Quae te frigore perculit Tanto bruma ferox? Quis Boreas gelu Nuper Sarmatico furens Te, Ficus, stygias iussit ad arbores Migrare: atque Proserpinae Lucos examinem visere luridos, Et furuas Erebi domos: Atque horrenda nigris antra paludibus? Extinctas precor, o, precor Nostri delitias, Pieris, hortuli Moesto squallida carmine Dic, & perpetuis obrue fletibus. Priscis non fuit hortulis Arbos Hesperidum dignior aspici, Auro tergeminis licet Diui fulua darent poma sororibus
units.tr: What fierce winter cold has struck you down, fig tree? What Boreas, raging lately with Sarmatian frost, ordered you to migrate to the Stygian trees, to visit the pale groves of Proserpina, the dark houses of Erebus, and the horrid caves amid black marshes? I beg, I beg, Pierian Muse, the dead delight of our little garden: tell it with a mournful song, and overwhelm it with perpetual tears. In ancient gardens no tree was more worthy to be seen than the tree of the Hesperides, though the tawny golden apples were given by the divine sisters, guarded by a watchful dragon posted as sentinel with rigid vigilance.

units.la: Quæ custos vigil additus Seruabat rigidis excubÿs Draco.
units.tr: Which the watchful dragon, set there as guardian, kept with rigid watches.

units.la: Quondam Romula non fuit Ficus nobilior, conscia quæ lupam Texit, quùm facilis sua Præberet geminis vbera fratribus.
units.tr: Once there was no fig tree more noble in the city of Romulus, the one that covered the she-wolf, when it readily offered its udders to the twin brothers.

units.la: Romæ fortia qui suis Struxere auspiciis mœnia maximæ Ficus nectare dulcior, Ficus Cecropio melle suauior.
units.tr: Fig tree sweeter than nectar, under whose auspices those who built the strong walls of greatest Rome raised them; fig tree sweeter than Cecropian honey.

units.la: Mites quæ sociis tulit Iucundis, reditus, charáque munera Autumnus simul vberes Fructus pomifero prodigeret sinu.
units.tr: Which bore mild returns and dear gifts for its pleasant companions, while Autumn with its fruitful bounty poured forth abundant fruits from its fruit-bearing bosom.

units.la: Ficus grandior Indica Latas quæ patulis frondibus explicans Umbras sæpe sodalibus Non ingrata meis otia præbuit:
units.tr: Fig tree larger than the Indian fig, which, spreading wide leaves, often offered shade and restful leisure to my companions, and not ungratefully.

units.la: Quùm torrere canicula Campos æstiferis cœperat ignibus Iam iam feruidior suas Messes agricolis fortibus apparans Annos nulla fuit magis Arbor digna senis viuere Nestoris.
units.tr: When the dog-star had begun to scorch the fields with summer fires, growing ever hotter, preparing harvests for the brave farmers: no tree was ever more worthy to live for the years of aged Nestor.

units.la: Hanc lugete cupidines, Lugete, o Veneres, & Charitum chori Hanc slete, o, Dryades simul, Quas syluæ recreant, umbriferum & nemus, Quas semperiuuat arbores Maturis grauidas cernere fructibus. Ast tu Delphice nunc iube Vt post fata bonas talis ad infulas Ficus carminibus meet Commedata tuis, gratáque manibus Umbras pallidulas ferat, Campis Elysij mollibus insita.
units.tr: Mourn for this one, Cupids, mourn, O Venuses, and you choir of the Graces. Weep for it together, O Dryads, whom the woods and the shady grove refresh, and who always delight to see trees heavy with ripe fruit. But you, Delphic god, now order that, after its fate, the fig tree, deserving good fillets, be honoured by your songs, and that, planted in the soft fields of Elysium, it bear pale shades grateful to the spirits.

units.la: IOANNI BAPTISTÆ ROTHANO AMICO DVLCISSIMO & Ecclesiastæ Geneuensi.
units.tr: TO JOHN BAPTIST ROTHANUS, MOST SWEET FRIEND AND MINISTER OF THE CHURCH AT GENEVA.

units.la: QVÆ nunc causa, precor, quæve negotia Te Rothane tenent tam procul ædibus Charis? ecquid abes iam nimium diu: Maiorésque trahis pollicito moras?
units.tr: What cause, I pray, or what business keeps you, Rothanus, so far from the house of the Graces? Surely you are now away too long, and do you drag out your delays longer than you promised?

units.la: Tandem, quæso, redi, protinus & fuge Deformata feris Gallica motibus Arua, & purpureas sanguine ciuium Vrbes, & rabidis stragibus horridas.
units.tr: At last, I beg you, return, and flee at once the Gallic fields disfigured by savage upheavals, and the cities purple with citizens' blood, horrid with raging slaughters.

units.la: Coniunx ingenuis orta parentibus, Et cui fida pio pectore castitas
units.tr: A wife born of free parents, in whose pious breast faithful chastity clings to the marriage bond,

units.la: Hæret connubij, te DalmontiaSuspirans querula voce suum petit.
units.tr: Dalmontia, sighing, seeks you with a plaintive voice, as her own.

units.la: Absentem soboles parvula te patremPoscit sæpe suum: te rogat ut tuosMaturęs reditus, matris & anxiosSoleris gemitus, dum timet, heu! tibi.
units.tr: Your little offspring often asks for you, its father. She begs that your return be hastened, and your mother's anxious groans, while she fears, alas, for you.

units.la: Commissus fidei grex ouium tuæTristis te revocat: teque bonos sibiSuccos Ambrosiæ syderea cupitPræbere, & nitidi pocula nectaris.
units.tr: The sad flock committed to your faith recalls you, and the heavenly one desires to offer you good juices of ambrosia and the cups of bright nectar.

units.la: Et desideriys ista fidelibusOmnis te repetit turba sodalium.Segnes tolle moras: ocyus ut mihiTe reddas animæ dimidium meæ.
units.tr: And the whole crowd of your faithful companions calls you back with longing. Put aside lazy delays, so that you may more quickly restore to me the half of my soul.
TO ZOILUS.

units.la: Bezæ nostra placent, vatum celeberrimus ille est.Nil mihi nunc tecum, liuida turba, vale.
units.tr: Our Beza pleases; he is the most celebrated of poets. Now I have nothing more to do with you, envious crowd. Farewell.
ANOTHER.

units.la: Qui meos blateras nitere versusMagni versibus aureis Horatí,Sic possis mihi semper inuidere.
units.tr: You who chatter that my verses shine less than the golden verses of great Horace, may you always be able to envy me in this way.
